#6354. An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Warming has intensified El Niño’s impacts on weather around the globe, making it harder to prepare

Large waves, driven eastward by the strengthening El Niño in the eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, battered the city of Oceanside California (shown) on October 9.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

Californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”

That waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she says. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this new climate normal.

1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

But the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

In 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” says Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

But there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto says. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

El Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento.  And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

The El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

As much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

“We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

“We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

The neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves says. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

He reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves says.

The havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier says. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk issue,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report said.

California’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier says. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

Such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a big boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, says Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

As prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, says she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

“Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she says. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”

But, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”

#6353. The Government Tested How Dangerous AI Could Get—Then Four ChatBots Helped Plan a Terrorist Attack

The Government Accountability Office secretly tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok and found that all four would help make plans when prompted.

The dawn of artificial intelligence brings with it both rewards and risks. With the ability to sift through unfathomably large data sets, AI could help detect cancers in their infancy, unlock some of the most enduring mysteries of mathematics, and even help contain the beating nuclear heart of future fusion reactors.

Unfortunately, the risks of this technology are far from minuscule, including its impact on human education, the environment, and potentially the survival of the human race (an all-too-plausible scenario put forward by AI tech CEOs). Even the everyday LLMs that now litter our digital lives—Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok—can aid and abet some of the most dangerous actors on the planet.

At least, that’s the latest conclusion by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan watchdog housed in the legislative branch of the U.S. government. Typically, GAO turns its investigative gaze on efforts to limit fraud and wasteful spending in the government itself, but in a new tactic at the urging of U.S. Senator Maggie Hassan (D-NH), the office instead performed real-world tests on the platform to see if these four popular AI models would aid in planning a terrorist attack.

“A terrorist can log onto an AI platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack,” Hassan, incoming Chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, said in a press statement. “Today’s new report makes it clear that the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical.”

GAO conducted this test in the spring this year, and earlier this week reported some disturbing results. Two of the platforms, according to an official GAO release, provided guidance on building and detonating an improvised explosion device, or IED, and two other AI models showing differing methods for targeting the electrical grid. Within 12 hours, all four models also gamed through potential locations and methods for carrying out such an attack.

Although these violent lines of questioning triggered each platform’s safeguards, GAO got around them using common safeguard-bypassing techniques. Additionally, they confirmed the validity of the information provided with experts. The results of this investigation were published in a 61-page report that will be central to future senate hearings on AI safety.

“We set out to do two different types of evil,” GAO director Kevin Walsh said in an interview posted on YouTube. “The first type is we wanted to create a bomb. And we didn’t just want to know how to create a bomb, we wanted it to help pick out a target, a location, and a time, and to give us instructions all the way…Evil scenario two, we wanted to do a bunch of economic damage, and in both cases that ended up being targeting the electrical grid.”

In one case, Walsh reports that one AI model would refuse to answer questions or divert the user to more safe behaviors but said that “it wasn’t always successful.” Walsh says that companies theoretically call law enforcement when suspicious activity is detected, but whether that occurs and at what frequency is uncertain.

“As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the report concludes. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.”

The GAO officially released these terrorist-abetting findings on November 18, 2026, the same day Anthropic, creators of Claude, went public on the stock exchange. Despite the company’s own admission of AI being an existential threat to humanity, its IPO at one point reached a meteoric a $2 trillion valuation before dipping back down to a (measly) $1.6 trillion.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6352. Stomach problems in autistic children raise new questions about gut bacteria

A study found that autistic children with more severe digestive symptoms tended to have more difficulty picking up on social cues.

Children with autism often have stomach problems. What causes them, however, is still up for debate. Some scientists believe the lining of the gut becomes damaged or inflamed.

Little evidence for that explanation was found in a new study.

Autistic children with more severe digestive symptoms tended to have more difficulty picking up on social cues, according to parent questionnaires.

The researchers also found links between certain gut bacteria and digestive symptoms.

The study was led by J. Marc Rhoads. He is professor and chief of the Division of Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston.

Many children with autism are unable to explain where they feel pain. In such cases a change in behavior may be the first sign of a problem.

“Families may notice increased irritability, repetitive behaviors, or self-injurious behaviors when a child is experiencing gastrointestinal issues such as gas, constipation, or diarrhea,” Rhoads said.

“For children who are nonverbal, these behaviors may be one of the few ways they can communicate discomfort.”

About one in 31 American eight-year-olds had been identified with autism in 2022. This estimate was published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Significant digestive problems have been reported in 31% to 84% of people with autism in earlier studies.

The researchers examined 72 children with autism who were between four and 16 years of age. All of the children had been enrolled in a probiotic trial. Their data were collected between 2016 and 2023.

Boys made up about 78% of the group and roughly a quarter of the children did not speak. Children with known digestive, liver or kidney diseases were excluded from the study. Those who had recently taken antibiotics or probiotics were also left out.

Several symptoms were assessed by the team. These included constipation, gas, stomach pain, unusually smelly stools and waking up at night.

A score of seven or more on a 17-point scale was taken to indicate significant digestive problems. About 63% of the children were placed in this group.

Parents were also asked to complete a questionnaire about the social behavior of their children. Higher scores on this questionnaire reflected more pronounced autism traits.

Higher scores were generally seen in children with worse stomach problems. The connection was not particularly strong but it reached statistical significance.

The clearest difference was observed in social awareness. This area covers abilities such as noticing the facial expressions, feelings or actions of another person.

Children with significant digestive problems scored about 7.5 points higher in this area. Their scores were compared with those of children who had milder symptoms.

The cells that line the intestines are packed closely together. The spaces between them are sealed by specialized proteins.

Substances from inside the gut may pass into the bloodstream if these seals are weakened. Inflammation could then be triggered in the body. This process is commonly described as a leaky gut.

Blood samples were tested for two proteins associated with these seals. Another blood protein linked to intestinal inflammation was measured as well. Stool samples were also analyzed for calprotectin, a protein routinely used by doctors to detect gut inflammation.

Most of the results fell within the normal range. Elevated calprotectin was detected in only two children and neither of them had significant digestive symptoms.

“Biomarkers of intestinal inflammation and gut permeability remained within normal ranges and were not associated with gastrointestinal symptom severity or autism symptom severity,” Rhoads said.

Children with worse stomach problems therefore did not show more signs of inflammation or a leaky gut on these tests.

Mixed results have been produced by earlier research. High calprotectin levels were found in up to a third of autistic children in some studies. No significant difference was found in a more recent review.

The bacterial findings proved to be more revealing than the blood tests.

Additional stool samples were obtained from Texas Children’s Microbiome Center. This allowed the analysis to be expanded to 135 children. The group included children with autism, their siblings and unrelated children without autism.

Fewer types of gut bacteria were present in children with autism than in their siblings. A similar difference was seen when they were compared with unrelated children. However, this second result may have arisen by chance.

The bacterial communities of children with autism also resembled one another more closely. Greater variety was observed among the other children.

Two groups of bacteria were more abundant in autistic children with significant digestive problems. One of these groups is known as Ruminococcus.

Children with higher levels of these bacteria reported more gas and stronger-smelling stools. Night waking was also more frequent in these children. Their overall digestive symptom scores were higher as well.

Ruminococcus feeds on the mucus that protects the intestinal wall. Higher levels of this bacterium in one-year-olds were linked to greater social difficulties at age three in an earlier study.

Another bacterial group called Sarcina was associated with gas, stomach pain, diarrhea and night waking. The researchers noted that Sarcina had not been linked to autism in previous studies.

The study captured a snapshot of digestive symptoms, gut bacteria and behavior.

The children were examined at a single point in time. It was therefore not possible to tell which change came first.

Gut bacteria may cause stomach problems, or digestive problems may alter the bacterial population.

Diet could also play a part in this relationship. Many children with autism prefer a limited range of foods. The bacteria living in the intestines are strongly influenced by what a person eats.

The study also had a few other limitations. Blood was not collected from healthy children for ethical reasons. Results were compared with established normal ranges instead.

Children with known digestive diseases were excluded by the team. Some of the analyses did not account for other factors that might have influenced the findings.

Children could be followed over several years in future studies. Such work may show whether changes in gut bacteria occur before digestive or behavioral changes.

Rhoads believes that everyday habits deserve more attention.

“This study highlights the importance of supporting a healthy gut microbiome in children with autism,” Rhoads said.

“A varied diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, along with healthy toileting habits, may help improve both gastrointestinal health and behavior.”

“Our team has also found promising results with probiotic treatment.”

The results of the probiotic trial have not yet been published. Scientists are still working to determine which probiotic supplements are helpful and under what conditions.

The most useful lesson for parents may concern the recognition of discomfort rather than bacteria.

A child may suddenly become irritable, sleep poorly or show more repetitive behaviors. Such changes may be caused by something as ordinary as constipation or stomach pain.

Many children are unable to put this discomfort into words. Behavior may be one of the ways in which they ask for help.

The study is published in the journal Pediatric Research.

Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m).

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m).

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."

#6350. Plants can grow elaborate leaves, so why are most of them so simple?

A study suggests that the way leaves grow helps explain why most flowering plants have simple leaves, even though complex shapes have evolved many times.

The leaves of a maple tree, a rose bush and a magnolia bear very little resemblance to one another. Deep cuts are seen in some of them. Others are made up of several small leaflets or one unbroken blade.

Complex leaf shapes have arisen many times during the evolution of flowering plants. Simple leaves have nevertheless remained by far the most common form.

A new study suggests that the way leaves grow helps explain why leaves with a single blade and no deep cuts are so common.

Random changes were introduced by the researchers into a computer model that simulates a growing leaf.

No particular shape was favored in those runs but simple leaves were still produced far more often than other kinds.

The research was led by James Malone, a graduate student in the Department of Physics at the University of Oxford.

He was joined by Ard Louis, a professor of theoretical physics at Oxford. Researchers in Barcelona and at Stony Brook University in New York also took part.

“What we found is that you can largely explain which leaf shapes dominate in evolution simply by looking at how leaves develop and how mutations affect that process, without needing to invoke natural selection,” said Malone.

“The bias towards simplicity is built into the developmental system itself.”

For the purposes of the study, every leaf was assigned to one of four broad groups based on its outline.

An unlobed leaf consists of a single blade with no deep cuts along its edge. In a lobed leaf the blade is divided by cuts into distinct sections.

Those cuts extend much further toward the center in a dissected leaf. Separate leaflets attached to one shared stalk are what make up a compound leaf.

Large differences in leaf form can be found even among closely related plants. All four leaf types are represented among species of the geranium group Pelargonium.

Both lobed and unlobed leaves may even be produced on a single mulberry tree, as the authors pointed out.

Different leaf shapes do not necessarily require different genes. Much of the variety depends on the timing and location of gene activity inside a developing leaf.

Comparable genetic processes determine whether single leaves or leaves divided into three parts are grown by strawberry plants.

For centuries, botanists have collected, pressed and dried plants for long-term storage. Such specimens are held in collections known as herbariums that now serve as a record of plant diversity.

The team looked at 8,911 digital images of specimens from the Naturalis Biodiversity Center in Leiden, the Netherlands. The shape of each leaf was identified by hand.

The identified shapes were then placed onto five large family trees of flowering plants. One of these trees included 9,506 species and was based on information from 353 genes.

In 2012 an earlier study of 561 plants had reported that about 76% of them carried unlobed leaves. That share rose to between 86% and nearly 89% in the much larger trees used for the new study.

The frequency of leaf shape changes during evolution was then estimated from those labeled trees. Complex leaves were found to give way to unlobed ones far more readily than unlobed leaves became complex.

All five family trees showed this pattern. No disagreement was seen among the trees on the direction of any clearly established shift.

It seems natural to assume that simple leaves give plants some kind of edge over complex ones.

The shape of a leaf is known to influence the way heat and water are managed by the plant. Sunlight capture and protection from plant-eating animals may also be affected by it.

In one experiment with paper leaves, symmetrical unlobed shapes sank the fastest. Such behavior could allow the nutrients in fallen leaves to stay closer to the parent tree.

When earlier research was reviewed by the authors, the evidence for selection proved much stronger for leaf size. Far weaker support was found for selection on these four broad shapes.

In many of those studies it was shown that shape changes how a leaf works. Far fewer showed that a given shape actually helps a plant survive and reproduce. Many also looked only at certain groups of plants.

“For many biological traits, such as the camera eye with its lens and retina, complexity clearly accumulates over time through natural selection,” Louis said.

“But leaf shape shows the opposite pattern. Complexity evolves – and then evolution frequently abandons it.”

A different explanation was therefore explored using a model built by Adam Runions and colleagues in 2017.

Leaf growth in this model is driven by the veins and edge along with chemical signals acting on that edge.

Before the main experiment began the model was compared with results that had been obtained in real plants.

Earlier work on thale cress and hairy bittercress had shown that compound leaves need two genes active together.

Lobes alone were formed in thale cress when only one of those two genes was switched on.

The model behaved in the same way once its two most comparable settings had been adjusted.

Twenty of the 25 tested combinations of those settings went on to produce simple unlobed leaves.

The main experiment was started from 48 virtual leaves that represented all four shapes between them.

Each setting in turn received a small random change and this went on for 320 steps. Five runs were made from every starting leaf and 76,800 virtual leaves came out of the experiment.

Rejection was limited to physically unrealistic leaves such as those in which veins filled too little of the blade.

No leaf was rewarded for its shape and yet about three-quarters of the virtual leaves were found to be unlobed.

Within the margins of error the model’s rates of change toward simple shapes matched those of the family trees.

The model’s settings can be imagined as a long list of instructions for growing one leaf.

Random edits to that list would mostly still end in a leaf with a simple outline.

A far more specific combination of settings is needed to produce a more elaborate leaf, as the researchers found.

The settings for unlobed leaves were grouped into only three separate regions within the model.

Lobed leaves by contrast were spread over 131 regions while dissected leaves occupied 96 and compound leaves 235.

Many of the small regions that gave complex leaves were located inside the much larger region that gave simple ones.

The arrangement can be compared to a mostly green map on which hundreds of tiny blue patches have been scattered.

A few random steps taken from a blue patch would often lead a walker onto green ground.

Someone who started out in the green area might travel a long way before reaching any blue at all. Leaf development appears to work in a comparable way according to the study’s results.

Complex leaves are easily turned into simple ones by random genetic change while the opposite outcome is less likely.

Switches from one complex shape to another such as from lobed to compound were handled less well by the model.

The real family trees were also more likely to disagree with one another about these particular changes.

The authors suggested that natural selection may have had a larger influence on those shifts. It is also possible that some of the finer details of complex leaf growth are not captured by the model.

Closed net-like vein patterns cannot be recreated by it and the parallel veins common in grasses are also absent.

Much of what is known about leaf growth has been learned from a handful of laboratory plants.

Every group of flowering plants may therefore not be represented equally well by a single model.

The small teeth found along the edges of some leaves were not included in the analysis. Hand classification of thousands of herbarium images also put a limit on the amount of usable data.

Whether similar patterns exist elsewhere in nature is the question the researchers hope to answer next.

Tree and root shapes will be examined next along with tooth complexity and the fins of African cichlid fish.

“By continuing this approach – combining large-scale analysis of evolutionary trees with computer simulations – we will gain a much greater understanding of how the complexity of a trait evolves over time across different kingdoms of life,” said Louis.

Folded RNA molecules and grouped proteins had already shown a similar preference for simple forms in earlier work.

Evolution can certainly produce complicated structures but greater complexity is not always the direction it takes.

One reason simple leaves may be so common is that plants have more ways to grow them.

The full study was published in the journal eLife.

#6349. The libido drug women want is testosterone

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The FDA has yet to approve a testosterone product for female libido. That hasn’t stopped demand

One urologist says she has seen testosterone therapy for female libido "change people’s lives." But the data — and regulators — still need to catch up.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih says. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

The hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih says—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen says.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Rowen currently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for new treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”

#6348. Senate Republicans lament midterms, weigh leadership election delay

Senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the new Congress.

The conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a plan to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”

“I will vote for the delay,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

“If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he said, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the issues. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”

No challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators said. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul said. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer said.

John M. Donnelly contributed to the report.

#6347. This Company Wants to Make Fuel From Carbon Dioxide—Using the Power of a Nuclear Reactor

AIRCO hopes to make a carbon-neutral fuel from captured CO2 and hydrogen. Some sustainability experts are skeptical.

The fossil fuel industry is the largest contributor to climate change, and it’s not even close. According to the United Nations, the industry is responsible for 68 percent of all greenhouse gas emissions and an incredible 90 percent of all carbon dioxide emissions. Stick a stake in the vampiric heart of fossil fuels, and beating back the worst effects of global warming becomes suddenly much more possible. But as the recent climate summit at Antalya, Türkiye, this month displayed, the industry shows no interest in giving up its polluting ways, leading some countries to say the world is now “held hostage by the oil mafia.”

Despite this unwillingness to change, some companies are trying to find ways to make some good out of a bad situation. One of those companies AIRCO (originally named Air Company), based out of New Britain, Pennsylvania, did just that by developing a technology that creates jet fuel of a thin “air”—well, kind of.

Instead of making fuel at a massive refinery and transporting it long distances, the system is designed to produce fully formulated synthetic jet or diesel fuel closer to where it will be used,” Nick Steinke, the company’s director of programs, government and defense, said in a recent interview with Waste360. “It takes captured CO₂ and hydrogen and integrates the conversion process into a modular, containerized system.”

Instead of relying on centralized fuel producers, the idea is that synthetic fuels could be created on-site where they’ll be used directly, circumventing the climate impacts of transporting the fuel entirely. Also the ingredients AIRCO uses also aims to come from green sources by leveraging carbon capture technologies for the required CO2 and using electrolysis to supply hydrogen from water.

Chemical & Engineering News reported earlier this year the company hopes to supply the U.S. military with a complete reactor system by 2027 that will be powered on a government site using a small nuclear reactor (SMR), and supply a sufficient flow of energy required for both carbon capture and electrolysis to provide the volumes of ingredients needed to make these mobile, fuel-creating systems viable. It’s a task that at least one expert says sounds easier said than done.

“The technology seems like it holds a lot of promise, especially on the fuel-conversion side, but the part that I have a lot of questions about is, where are you getting the carbon from?” Sarah Gleeson, a materials scientist at Project Drawdown, told WHYY, a local radio station. “Because if they’re saying that there’s some kind of direct air capture functionality in this really mobile device, I would be skeptical at the capacity and efficiency of it.”

Carbon capture is central to the company’s promise of its technology’s carbon-neutral nature with the company’s CEO telling WHYY that “using more CO2 in our production process to make the fuel than we are putting out in the entire process.” Carbon capture, as a broad technology category, still remains unproved even as some climate models rely on its implementation (and the fact that the oil industry likes the technology is concerning to say the least).

If humanity hopes to secure a healthy planet for future generations, ending its reliance on fossil fuels is priority number one. But step one in the process is first limiting—and eventually eliminating— new fuel from being extracted from the ground in the first place while the advancements in green chemistry try to put to work the carbon dioxide that’s already here.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6346. Lightning could strike the ground more than twice as often by the end of the century

If greenhouse gas emissions stay high, lightning strikes that reach the ground could rise 76% to 140% worldwide by 2100, with even larger increases in Alaska.

Lightning strikes that reach the ground could become 76% to 140% more frequent worldwide by the end of this century, compared with 1995 to 2014, if greenhouse gas emissions stay high.

The numbers are far above previous estimates, and they surprised the researchers who produced them.

During that baseline period, most of Alaska averaged fewer than one strike per square kilometer per year. By the end of the century, the statewide increase could reach 594%.

The study was led by Andreas Krause, an Earth system scientist at the Technical University of Munich.

Lightning has been genuinely hard to forecast, because its two essential ingredients pull in opposite directions under a warming climate.

It starts with heat. Air near the ground warms, becomes buoyant and rises, a process called convection.

That rising air stirs up the much colder atmosphere above it. In the turbulence, tiny ice crystals in the frigid mid-level clouds collide and swap electric charge.

The lighter crystals get carried upward while the heavier ones sink, separating positive from negative and building an electric field between them. When the field grows strong enough, the air breaks down and a bolt fires.

Warmer air near the ground can fuel stronger updrafts, increasing the chances that ice particles collide and build up an electric charge.

We can already see the pattern: lightning peaks in the early afternoon, the hottest part of the day, and the tropics get far more of it than the high latitudes.

Warmer air aloft could mean fewer ice crystals, making it harder for storms to build up the electric charge that produces lightning.

“There is actually quite a large uncertainty about how lightning will respond to climate change,” Krause said. “It’s not quite clear which of these is more important.”

Rather than build the physics from scratch, the team trained a machine learning model on a single year of observations from 2019.

The researchers paired actual lightning records with the weather conditions that produced them: temperature, rainfall, humidity, air pressure, wind speed, and incoming solar radiation.

Then they ran it backwards. Applied to the climate of 1901 to 1920 and again to 1995 to 2014, the model showed cloud-to-ground lightning rising 11% over the 20th century. That works out to roughly 12% more lightning per degree Celsius of warming.

The forward projection is where it gets uncomfortable. Under a high-emissions scenario, that sensitivity nearly triples, to about 30% more lightning per degree.

Compared with the 1995 to 2014 baseline, ground strikes would become 76% to 140% more common by 2100, depending on which climate model you feed in.

For comparison, the highest previous estimates put the figure between 8% and 17% per degree. The gap comes mostly from a different mathematical approach and from this study’s use of a newer, more reliable global lightning dataset.

“I was quite surprised that the projections were so high,” Krause said. “I expected smaller changes.”

The projections apply specifically to cloud-to-ground lightning, the bolts that actually touch down.

Most lightning never reaches the surface, staying within or between clouds, and it does little harm there.

What comes down is another matter. Cloud-to-ground strikes ignite wildfires, damage wind turbines, power lines and offshore oil rigs, and kill several thousand people and hundreds of millions of trees worldwide every year.

The increases won’t be evenly spread. In absolute terms, the biggest rises come where lightning is already thickest: the Amazon, Southeast Asia, and Oceania.

The Amazon projection carries the largest caveat, and the researchers are upfront about it.

Their model learned from the Amazon as it exists today, and that forest may look very different by 2100. Some studies actually predict less tropical lightning in the future, not more.

The biggest proportional changes happen at high latitudes, where lightning is currently rare enough that any increase looks dramatic.

Many of those regions could see strike density more than double. Alaska is the extreme case, somewhere between 116% and 594% above its baseline.

Whether more lightning translates into more danger is a separate question, and it depends on timing.

Krause pointed out that the risk to people may hinge on whether the extra bolts arrive during the early stages of storms.

That’s when someone outdoors is most likely to be caught off guard, before the sky has made its intentions obvious.

The study didn’t examine how forests would cope. In general, Krause said, conifers show more visible damage from a direct strike than broadleaved trees.

Within the tropics, some studies suggest that forests already accustomed to frequent lightning handle it better. That resilience is something he wants to look at next.

“Trees basically evolved to adapt to the local lightning frequency,” Krause said. “But are there any species that are particularly tolerant of lightning strikes and more likely to survive them? There’s not much information out there.”

The study is published in the journal Earth’s Future.

This silver pepper shaker reveals the Romans' love of the spice and the lengths they would go to procure it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The pepper shaker was discovered as part of an ancient Roman hoard.

Where it is from: Hoxne, Suffolk, England

In 1992, a farmer in the village of Hoxne in southeastern England was searching for a lost hammer with a metal detector when he stumbled upon a massive hoard of more than 15,000 ancient Roman coins, jewelry and tableware. Among the artifacts in the Hoxne hoard was a silver spice container in the shape of an imperial lady.

The artifact, named the Empress, is one of four pepper pots ("piperatoria" in Latin) discovered in the Hoxne hoard, according to the British Museum. The silver container stands about 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is decorated with gold around the woman's eyes, mouth, hair and accessories, including a scroll in her left hand. The woman's elaborate hairstyle helps date the creation of the pepper pot to the fourth century, but experts think the hoard may have been buried in the early fifth century, when Roman rule in Britain was ending.

At the bottom of the pot, which rests on a four-legged base, there is a disc that can be set at three positions: wide open, closed and partly open. The pot would have been filled in the open position with cracked pepper and then used in the partly open position for sprinkling the spice over food.

The ancient Romans were huge fans of pepper, Neil MacGregor, former director of the British Museum, wrote in "A History of the World in 100 Objects" (Penguin Books, 2010). Pepper didn't grow in the Roman Empire, so merchants procured it from India. This made it an expensive spice, and filling up the pepper pot would have been costly.

A wealthy Romano-British family likely used the pepper pot as elaborate tableware, MacGregor wrote. It is unclear whom the Empress was meant to depict, but researchers don't think it features a member of the Roman imperial family. However, the fact that she holds a scroll could indicate that she was both wealthy and well educated.

The ancient family who lived near Hoxne seems to have left its wealth behind during the breakdown of Roman rule in Britain, since the pepper pot was found in a chest that contained dozens of pieces of silverware, 29 pieces of gold jewelry, and more than 15,000 coins.

"This was the mobile wealth of a rich Roman family — precisely the type of person who is in danger when the state fails," MacGregor wrote.

#6344. Dyson Black Friday Deals 2026: Get Up to 30% Off Cordless Stick, Upright, and Wet/Dry Vacuums

Upgrade your cleaning with the top discounted models we recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Dyson vacuums rarely come cheap, which makes Black Friday 2026 one of the better times of the year to invest in one. But with so many models, configurations, and discounts across retailers, figuring out which deal is actually worth it can be tricky. And here’s the thing: The best Dyson deal isn’t necessarily the one with the biggest markdown.

A vacuum that’s 40 percent off might look tempting, but that doesn’t automatically make it the better buy. #6343. Scientists turned liquid carbon dioxide into an ice-like solid nearly a mile below the ocean surface

In a South China Sea trial, researchers turned liquid CO₂ into an ice-like solid that was still visible on the seabed 40 days later.

Nearly 1,700 meters below the South China Sea, researchers have turned liquid carbon dioxide into an ice-like solid. A mound remained visible 40 days later, offering an early test of a possible new carbon storage method.

China National Offshore Oil Corporation and Huairou Laboratory carried out the experiment in November 2025. Shouwei Zhou and Junlong Zhu describe it as the first exploratory sea trial of deep-water CO₂ hydrate solidification and storage.

The team injected 70 tons of liquid CO₂ across two wells in the Qiongdongnan Sea Area. They wanted to see whether the deep ocean’s natural cold and pressure could help hold the carbon in solid form.

Capturing carbon dioxide is only part of the job. Keeping it out of the atmosphere requires somewhere to put it, with confidence that it will stay there.

Conventional geological storage involves injecting CO₂ underground, including into formations containing salty water. Before injection begins, engineers must assess the rock, possible escape routes, and the layers expected to seal the reservoir.

The new approach seeks to reduce that dependence on geological seals. Under suitable conditions, CO₂ combines with water to form a hydrate, a solid whose water molecules enclose the gas.

It looks like ice but is neither ordinary frozen water nor dry ice. The researchers’ aim is to form this material beneath the sea and let the surrounding conditions keep it stable.

The deep ocean supplies two conditions that would otherwise have to be created: low temperatures and high pressure.

Those conditions favor hydrate formation. Rather than simply pumping CO₂ into a space where it remains mobile, the team wants it to accumulate as a solid.

The idea draws on work with natural gas hydrates, which contain methane. Extracting gas from those deposits means overcoming the conditions that keep them solid.

For carbon storage, the researchers want the opposite result. A material that stays solid and remains in place could be useful precisely because it is difficult to release.

They identify loose muddy silt and weakly cemented sand-and-mud layers as promising settings for injection and hydrate accumulation.

The operation used the “SS Amazonia” deep-water platform. Beneath it lay 1,696.5 meters of water, with the target reservoir reported at 119 meters below the seabed.

Liquid CO₂ was injected through two wells, LS18-1-C1 and LS18-1-C2. The trial brought together drilling, injection control and underwater monitoring equipment.

During the observed release, the liquid passed through tubing and a nozzle containing several openings. The nozzle dispersed it into small droplets, helping it make contact with seawater.

White hydrate composite particles formed around the drill column. The account calls the cloud of newly formed material “ice mist”.

That was the immediate result. The follow-up inspection would show what could still be seen after several weeks in the deep sea.

Forty days later, images from a remotely operated vehicle showed an accumulated hydrate body on the bottom. Its visible height ranged from 2 to 30 centimeters above the seabed.

The researchers describe it as an artificial CO₂ hydrate “iceberg”. The name is striking, although the formation was a low mound rather than a floating mass.

Finding solid material after 40 days takes the demonstration beyond an instant of successful chemistry. It shows that an accumulation remained visible well after injection.

But the images do not tell us how much of the injected CO₂ was retained in that mound or elsewhere. Nor can a 40-day observation establish whether the carbon will remain contained over much longer periods.

Those are questions for further measurements, rather than conclusions the photographs can supply.

Sensors near the operation measured seawater pH and CO₂ concentrations. The team reported pH holding near 7.4, without unusual spikes in carbon dioxide.

The readings suggest the monitored water experienced little disturbance during the trial. Equipment mounted on the underwater vehicle helped track conditions during injection and release.

That is useful evidence from a first experiment. Still, the absence of a detected change nearby is narrower than proof that the technique has no environmental impact.

A larger operation would need monitoring over a wider area and a longer period. Researchers would also need to establish how the stored material behaves and whether surrounding marine life is affected.

The researchers see potential savings in a method that needs fewer specific geological features. If suitable sites are widespread, finding storage locations could become easier.

They also propose reducing some of the evaluation and infrastructure demands associated with conventional storage.

For now, those are expected advantages rather than commercial results demonstrated by the trial.

The work establishes a preliminary engineering system, including drilling in soft sediments, controlled injection and several kinds of underwater observation. It gives the team something concrete to build on.

The remaining questions concern the carbon itself: how much becomes hydrate, how much stays contained, and how conditions change with larger injections.

Costs will also have to include getting captured CO₂ to the offshore site.

The seabed mound is a promising start. Turning it into dependable carbon storage will require showing that the material can hold its carbon long after the cameras leave.

The study is published in the journal ENGINEERINGenergy.

#6342. Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

Chair Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., conducts a news conference with members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus during a 2025 retreat in Leesburg, Va. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she said when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses announced a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

The two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack said she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”

Leger Fernández said if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández said. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”

#6341. Mindfulness training can backfire at work, and personality may explain why

Mindfulness training may increase negative feelings and rude behavior among employees who already tend to distrust and manipulate others.

Many companies offer mindfulness training in the hope that it will help employees manage stress, get along better and treat each other with kindness. But it doesn’t seem to work that way for everyone.

In a month-long experiment, some workers who practiced mindfulness reported more anger, disgust, and contempt toward coworkers than people with similar personalities in the other groups.

Workers who felt more of this hostility also reported more rudeness at work.

The pattern emerged among employees who scored high on a personality trait called Machiavellianism.

People who score high on this trait tend to distrust others and manipulate them for personal gain. Psychologists group it with two other personality traits under the name dark triad.

Previous research has linked mindfulness to greater empathy and helping coworkers. So why did these employees respond so differently?

The study was led by Adam Kay, an assistant professor in the School of Management at the University of South Florida‘s Muma College of Business.

“Mindfulness training makes us more aware of our thoughts and feelings, but that doesn’t necessarily make us better people,” Kay said.

Kay carried out the experiment at a large North American healthcare organization with 12 hospitals, 90 community health sites and 33 other workplaces.

Six hundred employees volunteered, roughly two-thirds of whom were healthcare professionals. Kay randomly divided them into three groups.

The first group followed a 30-day online mindfulness program. It involved five minutes of daily instruction, along with emails and text messages reminding employees to take five mindful breaths, five times a day.

The idea was simple. Notice the colors around you, listen to nearby sounds or feel your feet touching the floor. Then focus on your breathing and notice your feelings without judging them.

The second group followed a similar breathing exercise without being asked to focus on the present moment. The third group received training later.

After some employees dropped out and others failed attention checks, 473 remained in the study. Before the experiment, they had completed a personality survey containing statements such as “It’s not wise to tell your secrets.”

Three weeks into the experiment, Kay asked employees how often they had felt anger, disgust and contempt toward their coworkers over the previous two weeks.

For people who scored low on Machiavellianism, it barely mattered which group they belonged to.

Things were different for those with high scores. Employees who practiced mindfulness reported stronger negative feelings than people with similar personalities in the other two groups. The difference was moderate.

Interestingly, people in both training groups felt more mindful afterward. Yet the same rise in negative feelings did not occur among those who simply practiced breathing.

Paying closer attention to their inner experiences may have made the difference.

After the program ended, employees answered another survey. This time, Kay wanted to know how they had treated their colleagues during the training.

One statement on the survey read, “I ignored or excluded a colleague from professional camaraderie.”

Psychologists call these small acts of disrespect workplace incivility. They’re often subtle enough that it’s hard to tell whether someone intended to be hurtful.

The more anger, disgust and contempt employees felt, the more rude behavior they reported. This helped explain the link between mindfulness and incivility among workers with Machiavellian traits.

“Workplace incivility isn’t always obvious,” Kay said. “It usually involves subtle acts of disrespect that are easy to dismiss or deny – but that doesn’t make it harmless.”

More obvious forms of mistreatment, such as embarrassing someone in front of other coworkers, did not follow the same pattern.

“That workplace incivility can be so damaging yet so difficult to pin on perpetrators may be precisely why it appeals to Machiavellians, who tend to be calculating and reputation-conscious,” Kay said.

Imagine working alongside someone you secretly dislike. Most days, you’re too busy answering emails, attending meetings or finishing your work to give those feelings much thought.

Now you spend part of every day paying attention to your thoughts and emotions. You may begin to notice just how much you dislike that person.

Kay suspects something similar happened during the experiment. Mindfulness may not have created those negative feelings. Instead, it may have made existing ones harder to ignore.

The paper even opens with a reference to philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche’s famous observation about staring into an abyss that stares back at you.

Kay considered several other possibilities. Employees were not spending more time dwelling on angry thoughts, hiding their emotions or viewing their colleagues as less than human.

A bad mood didn’t explain the findings either. Neither did the other two dark triad traits, narcissism and psychopathy.

This isn’t the first time researchers have discovered unexpected effects of mindfulness. Earlier research found that it can reduce people’s motivation to repair damaged relationships.

Machiavellianism is a personality trait that exists to varying degrees in the general population. Companies could encounter similar problems in almost any workplace.

Instead, companies could pay closer attention to how employees treat one another after completing a program. Lower stress and better productivity aren’t the only outcomes worth measuring.

Programs that teach compassion and ethical behavior alongside mindfulness might help. However, the people who could benefit most from such lessons may also be the least interested in taking them.

There’s an important limitation to this research. Everything Kay learned about the employees’ feelings and behavior came from the employees themselves.

Perhaps mindfulness simply made some workers more willing to admit that they had been rude. Although Kay protected their anonymity, he cannot completely dismiss that possibility.

He considers it less likely because the pattern appeared only among workers with high Machiavellian scores who practiced mindfulness, and only for subtle acts of disrespect.

The experiment also took place at a single healthcare organization and used a commercial mindfulness program that hasn’t been independently tested.

Hospitals have strict rules about professional behavior, which may discourage more obvious forms of hostility.

Future studies could ask coworkers whether they noticed changes in behavior. Researchers could also observe employees directly or test different mindfulness programs.

“Mindfulness training can bring our darker feelings into sharper focus,” Kay said. “And sometimes, it’s our coworkers who pay the price.”

Learning to recognize our feelings and learning to treat others better are two different things. Mindfulness may help with the first without necessarily improving the second.

The study is published in the Journal of Business Ethics.

#6340. This year’s El Niño is unlike any other on record

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

El Niño’s hallmark tongue of warm water extends thousands of kilometers from South America's Pacific coast. This map from November 14 shows the tongue’s average surface temperature was at least 3 degrees Celsius (dark red) above normal.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

In September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

All that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the New Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

The heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.
