#6337. Habits like nail biting may be clues to hidden mental health struggles in teens

About one in eight students surveyed in England reported significant distress over nail biting, skin picking, or hair pulling.

Nail biting and skin picking are widely regarded as nothing more serious than bad habits. In a survey of students in England, most teens who reported these behaviors said they caused little or no distress.

The survey was answered by 5,437 students. More than half of them reported sometimes picking, pulling, or biting at their hair, skin, or nails.

The behavior was described as difficult to control, although little or no distress was reported by most of these students.

About one in eight students gave a different answer. These students said the behavior upset them quite a lot or a great deal. This distress was closely associated with anxiety, depression, and bullying.

The study was led by Clare Mackay, a professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Oxford. The behaviors are familiar to her from her own life.

Researchers have a name for them: body-focused repetitive behaviors, or BFRBs.

“BFRBs aren’t simply bad habits. They’re often signs that a young person is struggling,” Mackay said.

Because the students were surveyed only once, the answers can indicate which problems occur together. The order in which those problems appeared cannot be established from the data.

The questions formed part of the 2025 OxWell Student Survey, which reached 32,102 students in England.

A total of 49 secondary schools and colleges took part, and most were state schools in Oxfordshire and Merseyside.

The survey was usually completed online during a lesson. An optional set of questions was then offered, and some students continued to it.

Within that group, the questions about picking, pulling, and biting were answered by 5,437 students aged 11 to 18.

Three questions were written for the survey by Mackay’s team. Before being sent to schools, the questions were tried by 26 people with personal experience of the behaviors. Those people also commented on the questions.

In the first question, students were asked about picking, pulling, or biting at hair, skin, or nails. Only behavior that feels difficult to control was covered by this question.

In the second question, students were asked how much the behavior upset them. Four possible answers were offered, ranging from not at all to a great deal.

The third question asked whether the behavior interfered with home life, friendships, leisure activities, or classroom learning.

Overall, at least one such behavior was reported by 58.5% of the students. Nail biting was the most common at 43.6%. It was followed by skin picking at 31.3% and by hair pulling at 14.5%.

For most of these students, the behavior was not experienced as a source of distress.

Among students who reported a behavior, 35.2% said it didn’t upset them at all. Another 42.6% said it upset them only a little. One of the two highest distress ratings was chosen by the other 22.2%.

The researchers then focused on that smaller group. It was made up of 691 students, or 12.7% of everyone surveyed. The highest rating was chosen by 182 of them.

The lowest levels of distress were reported by students who only bit their nails. One of the two highest distress ratings was chosen by 11% of them.

The share was 29% among students who picked their skin. Among students who pulled their hair, a share of 37% was recorded.

Hair pulling and skin picking are listed as disorders in psychiatry’s diagnostic manuals. No separate category has been given to nail biting.

Considerable overlap between the behaviors was also observed.

At least one other behavior was reported by 84% of the students who pulled their hair. Among students who picked their skin, the corresponding figure was 76%.

The authors suggested that the behaviors may share one underlying process. On this account, they may not be separate conditions.

Interference with daily life was also reported more often for hair pulling than for nail biting.

Depending on the area of life, interference was reported by 5% to 13% of students who only bit their nails. For students who pulled their hair, the range was 18% to 39%.

At least one behavior was reported by 45.6% of boys and 64.6% of girls.

A third group consisted of 272 students who identified as trans or gender diverse, or who were unsure. Within that group, a share of 84.2% was recorded.

Distress was also lowest among boys. Distressing behaviors were reported by 5.6% of boys and 16.4% of girls. In the trans, gender-diverse, or unsure group, the figure was 25%.

The team then accounted for anxiety, depression, bullying, and age. The gaps between boys and the other two groups remained.

In studies of adults seen in clinics, about four women have been reported for every man with these conditions. A much smaller gap between girls and boys was observed among the students.

According to Mackay’s team, these behaviors had not previously been reported in trans and gender-diverse adolescents.

A standard 25-question checklist of anxiety and depression symptoms was also completed by the students.

Distressing behaviors were reported by 6.3% of students whose scores fell in the normal range. The share was 19.4% in the borderline range. In the highest range, which is labeled clinical by the checklist, it was 34.2%.

Distressing behaviors were also more common among students who reported bullying.

Among students who reported no recent bullying, 9.6% had distressing behaviors. A share of 27.1% was recorded among students bullied about once a week or more.

The team then analyzed these factors together. Anxiety and depression symptoms showed the strongest link to distressing behaviors. Gender and frequent bullying also remained linked.

Distressing behaviors were reported about twice as often by students who said they had autism, ADHD, or both. The comparison was made with students who reported neither condition.

Once anxiety, depression, gender, and bullying had been accounted for, that difference was no longer statistically significant.

The authors wrote that picking, pulling, and biting may work as a way of managing difficult feelings. The behaviors can then become a source of shame.

Young people may stay silent about the behaviors because of shame and stigma, said Polly Waite. For the same reasons, help may not be requested.

Waite is a co-author from Oxford’s Department of Experimental Psychology.

That question cannot be answered by the survey. Since each student answered only once, it cannot be shown whether anxiety leads to picking and pulling.

It is also possible that anxiety is increased by the behaviors.

Earlier work suggests that the relationship may run in both directions.

The students also may not represent English teenagers as a whole. Participation in the optional questions was a matter of choice.

Compared with the full survey, this group included more girls and gender-diverse students. Higher anxiety and depression scores were recorded in it as well.

As a result, students with emotional difficulties may have been over-counted.

The three questions are new and have not yet been formally tested. It also cannot be determined from them which students would meet the criteria for a diagnosis.

Mackay’s team wrote that these behaviors are rarely asked about in schools and clinics. A single screening question was therefore suggested by the authors.

It asks whether picking, pulling, or biting upsets a young person. It also asks whether the behavior stops them from doing things they want to do.

The next question is whether distress tied to these behaviors would be eased by reducing anxiety, depression, or bullying.

The authors wrote that this could be tested in future studies, especially among girls and gender-diverse young people.

The full study was published in the journal BMJ Mental Health.

#6335. How do tumors talk to nerves? This scientist is finding out

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Sebnem Ece Eksi wants to see how nerves change as cancer progresses. She hopes those changes could offer clues for detecting tumors earlier.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

The finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

“What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi says. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”

Eksi now plans to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

“This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi says. “It’s growing so quickly, the field itself.”

#6334. Ancient hunters in Australia had more on the menu than archaeologists expected

Ancient bones from two sites in northwestern Australia suggest that a varied diet gave hunters more options as rainfall and prey availability changed.

Ancient hunters in northwestern Australia ate a wide range of animals, and their leftovers suggest they could be choosy.

A study spanning roughly 50,000 years found that dietary variety could reflect plentiful food and skilled hunting.

The research was led by Tiina Manne from the University of Queensland. Her team examined ancient animal remains from Riwi rockshelter and Boodie Cave on Barrow Island.

A widely used archaeological model predicts that hunters first concentrate on prey offering the greatest returns. They add less rewarding animals when preferred foods become harder to obtain.

The new research challenges that reading of dietary diversity. At both Australian sites, people ate many kinds of animals from early in the occupation records.

“First Nations peoples in Australia were much more sophisticated and strategic in the animals they chose to hunt,” Manne said.

“Flexibility, not fixation on a few species of prey, was the smartest way to live in an unpredictable climate.”

Riwi stands on Gooniyandi traditional lands near the Great Sandy Desert. People began using the rockshelter about 45,000 years ago.

Its deposits contain remains of wallabies, echidnas, possums, flying foxes, lizards, and snakes. Small wallabies, lizards, and snakes dominate the earliest part of the analyzed sequence.

Boodie Cave’s first occupation dates to between about 51,100 and 46,200 years ago. Barrow Island was then part of the mainland, with its surroundings changing as sea levels fell and rose.

The team identified 1,167 specimens from Riwi and 2,083 from Boodie Cave by animal group or body size. The varied diets persisted across substantial environmental changes.

Burned bones and impact marks at Riwi helped link the remains to human food preparation. Some fractures also occurred while the bones were fresh.

“In a land of unpredictable rainfall, a variety of foods signal ‘plenty’, and flexibility was the best strategy,” Manne explained.

Some of the most revealing findings were bones still joined together, known as articulated remains. Their condition suggested that people had discarded body parts with little nutritional value.

“On Barrow Island, which was then connected to the mainland, the diet included wallabies, turtles and reef fish, and articulated bones suggest only the most nutritious parts were eaten and the rest were discarded,” Manne said.

“This isn’t the behavior of people short of food – they could afford to be choosy, so a broad diet reflected choice, not scarcity.”

The paper dates these articulated remains to around 7,200–6,800 years ago, long after the earliest occupation. Around this time, rising seas were cutting Barrow Island off from the mainland.

The researchers documented 24 groups of joined bones, including fish spines and parts of turtle limbs.

They interpret these discarded portions as evidence that people could select the more rewarding parts of their catches.

An animal’s value depended on more than its size. Weather affected both its condition and the effort needed to catch it.

“When water and vegetation were plentiful, large kangaroos were spread thin across the landscape, but in arid conditions they became easier to ambush as they stayed near waterholes,” Manne said.

“Small animals like bandicoots were also a good option when it got dry, because they stayed fat by switching to eating insects.”

“Hunters who kept their options open could shift between prey as conditions changed.”

At Riwi, large kangaroo remains became prominent after about 34,000 years ago, as conditions grew drier. The authors suggest hunting them became less risky when water drew the animals into more predictable locations.

Fat mattered, too. Opened leg bones at both sites point to the extraction of marrow, while smaller insect-eating animals could retain valuable fat during drought.

Many Australian animals hide in burrows, vegetation, or rock crevices during the day. Finding them requires knowing which traces to follow.

The paper draws on First Nations ecological knowledge, including signs such as fresh tracks, disturbed soil, and scratches on bark. These can reveal prey that a hunter cannot see directly.

“A tremendous amount of ecological knowledge is passed on in oral histories, including subtle signs of not only how to find prey, but the best prey depending on the season and circumstances,” Manne said.

Where hidden animals were abundant and diverse, investigating those signs could reward hunters with many different foods. A smaller animal could be a dependable catch even when a larger one promised more meat.

The authors argue that archaeological diets need to be understood through local animal behavior, food availability, and hunting costs.

A fixed ranking of desirable prey can miss how those factors change with rainfall.

Animal remains also reveal only part of a meal. Plant foods, documented at other northern Australian sites, would have supplied important carbohydrates alongside meat and fat.

“Importantly, our work suggests archaeologists around the world should re-consider how they have interpreted diet choice and diversity,” Manne concluded.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the Natural Academy of Sciences.

Archaeological discoveries can offer remarkable insights into the lives, cultures and beliefs of ancient peoples. From richly furnished royal tombs to caches of silver coins, some of the most significant finds have revealed how people lived, traded, fought, governed and died thousands of years ago.

Other discoveries stand out for their extraordinary preservation or historical significance. For example, the most expensive shipwreck on record — the 300-year-old Spanish galleon San José that's worth an estimated $17 billion — was found off the coast of Colombia in 2015 and continues to inform archaeologists and challenge governments that can't agree about its modern ownership. Meanwhile, ancient texts can provide invaluable clues about long-lost languages and civilizations. The Rosetta stone opened up the world of ancient Egypt to scholars, but researchers are still trying to decipher the mysterious Indus Valley script, one of the world's earliest urban civilizations.

#6332. Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

California Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#6331. Virtual reality can make you feel sick even when the scene around you stays still

In a five-minute VR experiment, watching a single moving ball increased nausea, eye discomfort, and disorientation as the eyes aimed and focused at different distances.

Volunteers spent five minutes in a virtual reality headset watching a speckled ball glide toward them and away against a black background. Afterward, they reported more nausea, eye discomfort, and disorientation than before.

The ball was designed to put two jobs the eyes normally do together at odds.

As it appeared to move closer, the volunteers’ eyes turned inward to follow it, but the headset kept the image in focus at a fixed distance.

A cap of 64 electrodes recorded their brain activity shifting while it happened.

The research was conducted by Mattie Johnson, a computer science doctoral student at the University of Maryland.

Amitabh Varshney, a computer science professor and dean at the university, led the study, and Sujal Bista of the University of Maryland Institute for Health Computing was a co-author.

The team worked with the Food and Drug Administration and Sony on the study.

The team is careful about what the electrode readings mean. The scene used for comparison differed from the test scene in more than one way, and the authors can’t fully rule out eye and facial muscle activity.

So the paper calls the brain changes candidate correlates, not a signature of this kind of sickness.

Look at a real object and your eyes do two things at once: they turn inward to aim at it, and their lenses adjust to bring it into focus.

The two distances agree. A headset breaks the agreement. Its screens sit at one fixed focal distance while the 3D picture asks the eyes to aim nearer or farther.

The Meta Quest 2 used here has its focal plane about 4.3 feet (1.3 meters) in front of the eyes. The team measured that with a camera and a test pattern.

Within about half a diopter of that distance the mismatch is mild. Outside it, discomfort builds.

So the team showed volunteers a black-and-white speckled ball on a black background. It glided from 11 inches (0.275 meters) out to 4.7 feet (1.425 meters) and back, one round trip every 3.9 seconds.

The ball grew as it receded and shrank as it approached, so it always looked the same size.

The researchers designed the scene to reduce the feeling that viewers themselves were moving while still making their eyes aim nearer and farther.

Forty people, 65% of them men and nearly all between 18 and 30, took part.

The researchers analyzed brain recordings from 38 people and complete questionnaires from 38 people. Each analysis excluded a different pair of participants.

Each person sat through five minutes with eyes closed, five minutes looking at a headset’s static home screen, and then five minutes of the moving ball.

Before and after the ball, they filled out a 1993 simulator sickness questionnaire, the SSQ. It scores nausea, eye-related symptoms, and disorientation.

All three scores rose, and the total score rose by what statisticians call a large effect. Men and women both reported more symptoms, though men’s disorientation scores didn’t rise by a reliable amount.

Most participants described themselves as not at all or only slightly prone to this kind of sickness.

The electrode cap sampled the scalp 250 times a second. Software stripped out blinks and muscle noise as best it could.

The team compared 50 seconds of brain activity near the end of the home-screen baseline with 50 seconds near the end of the moving-ball scene.

In clusters of activity toward the front of the head, power in the fast beta and gamma brain waves fell. In clusters toward the back, power in the slower theta waves fell.

“In the frontal lobe, we found a statistically significant decrease in high brain wave frequencies during cybersickness, and in the occipital lobe we saw a statistically significant decrease in low brain wave frequencies,” Johnson said.

“These changes in what we call EEG clusters could be useful predictors of a cybersickness experience.”

The pattern is not the one Varshney’s group found in 2022 for the motion kind of virtual reality sickness, where slower waves grew stronger over the center of the head.

The studies found different patterns, but the researchers still don’t know whether the latest pattern reflects sickness, differences between the scenes, or both.

The baseline scene and the ball differed in brightness, content, and layout. Volunteers were told where to look during the ball but not during the baseline.

Some of the drop in slow waves at the back of the head may simply be visual processing of a different picture. The front of the head is also where eye movements leak into recordings most.

The team didn’t record whether participants wore glasses or contacts, and nearly everyone was under 30.

The authors also wrote that the headset’s three fixed lens-spacing settings fit a larger share of women than men poorly. That could add to symptoms in ways the study can’t separate.

Whether the brain changes track the sickness itself, the change of scenery, or both is the question the authors leave open.

Settling it would need a baseline scene matched to the test scene, which the authors recommend. It would also need eye tracking to remove the eyes’ own electrical traces, which Johnson’s team plans to add.

The goal beyond that is a headset that detects the pattern and adjusts the scene.

“Ultimately we want to inform technology to mitigate symptoms in real time, improving user comfort and productivity over extended periods of immersion,” Johnson said.

Bista put it as a shift in who gets asked.

“The SSQ still has its uses, but now we have the tools to go from asking participants how they’re feeling to asking the brain and body what’s really going on,” he said.

The full study was published in the journal Virtual Reality.

#6329. How do scientists learn from failure? This researcher has clues

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Cornell computational social scientist Yian Yin turns the tools of science on science itself. He’s studying how AI-assisted submissions are changing what gets through peer review.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” says Yin, of Cornell University.

He applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin says, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”

More recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the issue in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin says.

#6328. In 1950, Michigan beat Ohio State in the Snow Bowl without a first down, and the blizzard behind it dumped up to 62 inches of snow

The Snow Bowl storm, later called the Great Appalachian Storm, contributed to at least 160 deaths and is the worst Ohio Valley snowstorm NOAA has analyzed.

On the Saturday after Thanksgiving in 1950, Ohio State and Michigan played their annual game in Columbus in a blizzard. At noon, the temperature at the city’s airport, a few miles from Ohio Stadium, was 10°F, and visibility was half a mile.

Michigan won 9-3. It did so without a single first down and without completing a pass, according to the National Weather Service. The game became known as the Snow Bowl, and some call it the Blizzard Bowl.

The storm that buried the field was much bigger than one football game. Over the following days, it dropped as much as 62 inches of snow in West Virginia, sent temperatures down to 3°F in Atlanta, and pushed hurricane-force gusts into the Northeast.

It ranks as the worst Ohio Valley snowstorm analyzed by scientists at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

The game’s place in history has little to do with the quality of the football, the weather service’s office in Wilmington, Ohio, says.

It is remembered for “the weather, as the game was played in a significant blizzard unlike any that either school had played in before, or since.”

Neither team could move the ball, so they kept punting it away. Michigan punted 24 times, and its total offense for the whole game was 27 yards. Ohio State punted 21 times, and four of those punts were blocked by the Wolverines.

All of the scoring came from blocked kicks. Ohio State blocked a punt that led to a field goal. Two of Michigan’s blocks led to a safety and a touchdown.

“It speaks to the severity of the storm, the remarkable conditions, and just how debilitating extreme weather can be,” the Wilmington office wrote.

The weather service has analyzed the afternoon’s hourly observations at Port Columbus Airport. The temperature climbed only from 10°F at noon to 16°F at 4 p.m.

Sustained winds blew at 17 to 22 mph, with gusts of more than 35 mph, so wind chills stayed between -8°F and -1°F. Visibility dropped as low as a quarter of a mile in snow and blowing snow.

Two days earlier, the weather had been very different. On Thursday evening, November 23, which was Thanksgiving Day, it was 39°F in Columbus at 8 p.m.

An arctic cold front then moved through, and by midnight it was 20°F. By 7 a.m. on Friday, the temperature had fallen to 8°F.

On the day of the game, 7.5 inches of snow fell on Columbus. The weather service says that is still the city’s record for a single November day.

From Thursday night to the following Tuesday, the city got 14.9 inches. Its November 1950 total of 15.2 inches remains the snowiest November on record there.

The cold front that arrived on Thanksgiving night was the precursor to the Great Appalachian Storm of 1950.

According to the weather service office in Jackson, Kentucky, the arctic air behind it sent temperatures to all-time November lows across the Upper Midwest and the Ohio Valley.

Chicago dropped to -2°F on November 24, tying its lowest November reading, and the next day Louisville hit -1°F and Lexington -3°F, both records for the month.

On November 25, low pressure formed over the Carolinas, the Jackson office says. It moved northwest into Ohio by the middle of the next day, spreading heavy snow as it went, then spun over Lake Erie before it weakened and left for Canada on November 29 and 30.

The snow piled up from western Pennsylvania deep into West Virginia. Several places received more than 50 inches, and Coburn Creek, West Virginia, reported the largest total, 62 inches, according to NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI). Pittsburgh got about 30 inches.

The cold reached far into the South. Temperatures fell to 22°F in Pensacola, Florida, 5°F in Birmingham, Alabama, 3°F in Atlanta and 1°F in Asheville, North Carolina, NCEI says, and the record cold damaged crops in Georgia and South Carolina.

The storm drew arctic air in on one side and warm Atlantic air in on the other. While Pittsburgh was buried under snow at single-digit temperatures, Buffalo, New York, about 200 miles to the north, had temperatures in the 40s and no snow at all, the Jackson office says.

In the Northeast, the problem was wind. New York City recorded a gust of 94 mph, and Newark, New Jersey, 108 mph. Bear Mountain, just north of New York City, had a 140 mph gust, and Mount Washington in New Hampshire reached 160 mph.

The winds caused extensive tree damage and power outages, and coastal flooding that broke through dikes at LaGuardia Airport and flooded its runways.

Fierce winds are still a feature of big East Coast storms, as earth.com saw when blizzard winds battered the coast in a more recent storm.

Heavy rain on the warm side of the storm brought near-record flooding to eastern Pennsylvania. Then, in the first week of December, unusually warm weather melted the snow quickly. The Ohio River rose to 28.5 feet in Pittsburgh and 56 feet in Cincinnati, 4 feet above flood stage in both cities.

The storm contributed to at least 160 deaths, NCEI says. Insurance companies paid out more for its damage than for any earlier storm or hurricane, according to the Jackson office. They call it the costliest storm on record up to that time. NCEI describes it as one of the costliest storms on record.

NCEI rates major snowstorms with its Regional Snowfall Index, which combines how much snow fell, how large an area it covered and how many people lived there.

The 1950 storm scored 34.7 in the Ohio Valley, the highest of the 232 storms analyzed there. The second-worst, in March 1993, scored 24.6. In that region, more than 6.1 million people lived where at least 18 inches of snow fell.

In the Northeast, it ranks ninth of 230 storms, just behind the storms of February 2003, February 2010 and January 2016.

Scientists are still studying how storms like this work. NASA-backed scientists have flown research planes straight into snowstorms to learn how their heaviest bands of snow form.

The information was obtained from the National Weather Service’s pages Snow Bowl – November 25, 1950 (Wilmington, Ohio) and The Great Appalachian Storm of 1950 (Jackson, Kentucky), from NOAA NCEI’s article The Great Appalachian Storm in Historical Context, and the Michigan vs. Ohio State team game records of the University of Michigan’s Bentley Historical Library and the Ohio State University Archives.

The BepiColombo spacecraft has overcome a last-minute computer glitch to enter orbit around Mercury — the 2nd craft in history to orbit the closest planet to the sun.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update: On Tuesday (Nov. 24) ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher announced on X that the BepiColombo team has isolated the computer glitch, and tweaked the mission accordingly. "The remaining manoeuvres have already been replanned, with no extra burns needed," Aschbacher said. The two probes are still on track to seprate on Dec. 9. (This article was updated at 11:40 a.m. ET on Nov. 24).

After eight years slingshotting around the inner solar system, the joint European-Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo has finally entered into orbit around Mercury — becoming only the second mission ever to orbit the closest planet to the sun.

Mission scientists confirmed on Saturday (Nov. 21) that the spacecraft reached Mercury's orbit and is transmitting data back to the ground team.

However, the orbital insertion didn't go entirely as planned, European Space Agency (ESA) representatives said in a statement on Monday. Due to a software glitch, the spacecraft didn't fire its thrusters for the full 37 minutes required to slow its approach to Mercury.

ESA has investigates the issue and confirmed the spacecraft's new trajectory; meanwhile, BepiColombo remains "safe," the statement noted. The spacecraft should be ready to begin a year of intensive science observations of Mercury starting a few months from now.

An illustration of BepiColombo approaching Mercury for orbital insertion.

Built jointly by ESA and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), BepiColombo is actually two separate probes, which are currently stacked one atop the other in orbit. The ESA-built orbiter, named the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), and the JAXA-built orbiter, the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), carry separate science instruments, and they will soon diverge into separate orbital paths around the mysterious inner planet, operating as two probes gathering different streams of data.

A selfie of BepiColombo during a flyby of Mercury's north pole in 2025.

The pair of probes launched together aboard an Ariane 5 rocket in October 2018, and spent the following eight years on an interplanetary journey that took them past Earth, the moon and Venus. It even passed by Mercury itself six times. (During one of these flybys, in January 2025, Bepi snapped an incredible closeup photo of Mercury's north pole.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This complicated cosmic choreography was necessary to prevent BepiColombo from picking up too much speed and overshooting Mercury's orbit, according to ESA. Mercury sits about 36 million miles (58 million kilometers) from our star, or roughly one third of the distance between Earth and the sun. That makes it very difficult for a spacecraft to reach Mercury without being captured by the sun's considerable gravitational pull and dragged off course.

Only one other spacecraft — NASA's MESSENGER probe — has succeeded in entering Mercury orbit before, circling the planet from 2011 to 2015 after its own seven-year journey through space.

BepiColombo will spend the next few months getting both probes in position to start mapping Mercury in the greatest detail ever.

MPO and Mio are expected to separate in early December, with Mio entering a highly elliptical orbit around Mercury's poles. MPO will then take a few more months to fine-tune its trajectory, reaching a lower and more circular polar orbit in March 2027, according to ESA. Its science operations are expected to begin in April.

The sibling probes will each orbit Mercury several times a day, with MPO completing an orbit every 2 hours or so. Observing the mysterious inner planet from several different vantage points, the probes will make the most comprehensive map of Mercury ever. The mission's suite of science instruments will study the planet across the electromagnetic spectrum, taking observations in X-rays, gamma-rays and ultraviolet light, as well as collecting detailed measurements of the planet's magnetic field.

With this information, scientists hope to unravel many mysteries of the least-explored planet in the solar system. The new data should enable scientists to tackle myriad long-standing questions: What is Mercury's interior made of, and where does its magnetic field come from? How was the planet formed, and to what extent is it still tectonically active today? By making precise measurements of the spacecraft's orbit and position, a radio experiment will also provide a new test of Einstein's theory of general relativity.

Stay tuned for more updates from ESA about humanity's first visit to Mercury in more than a decade.

#6326. Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep. Celeste Maloy, R-Utah, walking alongside him. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, said they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”

The new leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

#6325. Would we know if lab-grown brain tissue became conscious?

Scientists propose testing whether lab-grown brain tissue can learn a pattern and detect when it changes, a possible clue in the search for signs of consciousness.

Scientists can grow small clusters of human brain cells in a dish. One set of joined clusters has reacted to capsaicin, the compound found in chili peppers, but a reaction like that doesn’t show the tissue feels anything.

Two neuroscientists have now proposed a way to check what such tissue, called a brain organoid, can do. Their plan borrows tests already used on infants, sleeping people, and patients who can’t respond.

The tests ask whether an organoid can learn a pattern and notice when the pattern is broken. The proposal reports no results, and the authors wrote that it is highly unlikely today’s organoids are conscious.

Lucia Melloni of Ruhr University Bochum in Germany and Stanislas Dehaene of the Collège de France in Paris wrote the proposal. Both belong to a brain and consciousness research program at CIFAR, a Canadian research organization.

“I don’t believe that brain organoids currently possess consciousness,” Melloni said.

“But given the pace with which the technology is advancing, they may do so in future. That’s why we need to start thinking about how we can find out.”

Organoids are grown from human stem cells. The cells organize themselves into tiny tissues that copy some features of the early developing brain.

Researchers can also fuse several organoids into what they call an assembloid. The one that reacted to capsaicin joined four organoids to rebuild a basic pain pathway.

“A reaction, however, is not proof that the tissue feels anything,” Melloni said.

Other teams have wired brain cells into machines, including one hooked to a simplified version of the video game Pong. Melloni and Dehaene wrote that those setups are too complex to show what the living tissue itself worked out.

In a 2024 study they cited, a gel that responds to electricity produced similar results in place of the cells.

The central test comes from research on how people process sequences.

A person hears ba-ba-ba-ba-bu again and again. The brain reacts to the bu because it differs from the four sounds before it.

After many repeats, the person learns the whole pattern. If the sequence then comes as ba-ba-ba-ba-ba, the brain reacts again, this time because the expected bu is missing.

The second reaction is the harder one. It depends on a memory of the whole sequence, built up over many repeats.

An organoid has no ears, so researchers would use electrical pulses or light in place of sounds.

They would stimulate two or more separate groups of cells in sequence and record how the tissue’s activity changes.

The question would be whether the same sequence produces a different response depending on what came before it.

Monkeys can learn patterns like this one too. That has let researchers study the brain activity behind the reactions in animals that have no language.

In people, the first kind of reaction survives sleep and anesthesia. The second seems to require a person to be awake and paying attention.

Doctors have also tried the test on patients who can’t communicate. In those patients, 80% of the ones whose brains showed the second reaction later regained consciousness.

The test missed many others. Only 35% of the patients who recovered had shown the reaction.

Melloni and Dehaene wrote that no single test would be enough. Their confidence would rise if an organoid passed this test along with several other known signs of consciousness.

The authors wrote that a failed test is perhaps the more likely outcome. A failure would lower confidence that an organoid is conscious.

Dehaene has a financial interest in this kind of testing. He is a co-inventor on a patent for methods to monitor consciousness and an associate at a company that uses those methods in clinics.

The authors wrote that there is no evidence current organoids hold any rich picture of the outside world or of themselves. The tissues are tiny, and they are cut off from a body and from surroundings.

Organoids can be kept alive for months to years, though, and they keep changing as they age. The authors proposed running the same tests on an organoid again and again as it matures.

Human babies show the second kind of reaction at 3 months of age, and it may be present before birth, after 35 weeks of pregnancy.

Repeated testing would show when each ability appears in an organoid.

The authors also wrote that if several signs ever pointed the same way, the ethical treatment of these tissues should change with the evidence.

Melloni and other researchers have called for an international board to oversee organoid research.

The full study was published in the journal Neuron.

#6323. A morning dose of blue light may help you sleep better at night

Office workers given morning blue light for 30 minutes slept about 11 minutes longer that night and brought more energy to work the next day.

Blue light has become the villain of bedtime. Phones get dimmed at night and glasses that block it sell as sleep aids.

Yet the same light, delivered for half an hour after waking, made a group of office workers sleep longer and better that night. The gain carried into the next day’s work.

The effect was modest, about 11 minutes more sleep a night and a small lift in how well people said they slept.

Participants who reported sleeping better also reported more alertness and less mental fatigue the next day. Greater alertness was linked to more engagement at work.

Kathleen Keeler, who studies management and human resources at Ohio State University’s Fisher College of Business, led the study.

Christopher Barnes of the University of Washington’s business school and Brian Gunia of Johns Hopkins University’s Carey Business School were among her co-authors.

The glasses came from a company called Ayo, which donated half the pairs used.

Barnes said the mechanism is not a morning jolt from the blue light itself. “It’s that the blue light helps them sleep better later that night, which helps them the following day,” he noted.

The body runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle that decides when a person feels sleepy and when they feel awake.

Light is the strongest signal that keeps that internal clock on time, and blue light, in particular, is what the clock responds to most.

Blue light at night pushes the clock later and holds back melatonin, the hormone that brings sleep on.

That is the part everyone has heard. The same light in the morning pulls the clock earlier, which, in principle, should make sleep come sooner and run smoother that night.

Workplace researchers had tested the night half of that idea with blue-blocking glasses and found better sleep and better work. Workplace studies had not tested the morning half.

The team invited 200 full-time employees at a large Midwestern university, all working roughly nine to five, and 182 finished the study.

Nearly three in four were women, and the typical participant was in their early forties. They had been with the university for about a decade on average.

For 10 workdays, each wore glasses that shine blue-turquoise light toward the eyes for 30 minutes right after waking, between 5 and 10 a.m. On average they started just before 7 a.m.

For one of the two weeks the blue glasses ran at full power. For the other they ran at 1%, a glow so faint that in earlier tests people couldn’t tell the two settings apart.

Which week came first was decided at random, so every person served as their own comparison.

Participants filled in a survey each morning about the night’s sleep and their energy, and another each afternoon about their work, from engagement to helping coworkers to slacking off.

The team collected 1,259 daily surveys and registered its predictions in advance.

Each participant kept the glasses and a year of the companion app afterward.

After a full-power morning, people reported sleeping about 11 minutes longer that night, and rated the night’s sleep about 3.5% higher. Neither number is large. The team then traced the effect through the next day.

Longer and better sleep predicted more alertness the next day, and better sleep predicted less of the feeling that one’s mental energy is running low.

Alertness, in turn, predicted stronger work engagement and more helping behavior. Less depletion predicted better task performance and fewer behaviors like taking an overlong break.

Each link in that chain was small, and the team said so.

“This is a pretty small, cheap, easy intervention, and we’re getting meaningful movement on work outcomes that matter,” Barnes said.

The morning blue light didn’t increase alertness that same day.

Alertness that same day was no higher, which is why the authors read the whole effect as running through sleep.

The benefit also built across the week rather than appearing in full on day one.

Two groups gained more than the rest. People who arrived with existing sleep problems saw a bigger improvement in sleep quality.

Younger employees saw a bigger gain in sleep length, with effects on engagement and helping that the older workers did not show.

The authors tied the age gap to the eye’s declining sensitivity to light with age, and called both findings exploratory.

Barnes had a cheaper suggestion. “The best thing you could do in the morning is get outside,” he said.

Every measure here was self-reported, including how well people said they performed, so the findings wait on a replication with objective records.

Everyone studied worked daytime hours at one university, and most were women. The authors said shift workers, who often miss morning light altogether, might gain more, but no one in this study worked nights.

The measure of workplace misbehavior was also short and noisy, which the authors said may have hidden a larger effect rather than created a false one.

What the glasses add on top of a sunny walk is the open question, since the study compared bright glasses with dim ones, not glasses with daylight.

The authors said the next test belongs with people whose schedules fight their body clocks.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Applied Psychology.

#6322. A golden bar of stars cuts through the heart of a spiral galaxy

Hubble’s portrait of NGC 4394 shows how a bar of stars fits into a spiral galaxy and offers a rare perspective on the structure of our own Milky Way.

Today’s Image of the Day features a nearly face-on view of the spiral galaxy NGC 4394.

A pale gold bar stretches across the galaxy’s bright core, while thin lanes of dust curve around the center. Farther out, two spiral arms sweep into the dark.

That angle makes the bar easy to spot and gives us something we can only imagine for our own Milky Way: a view down onto the disk, with the center and the spiral arms visible in the same frame.

The European Space Agency released this Hubble Space Telescope image on November 24.

The galaxy lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Its light was already on its way here long before humans appeared on Earth.

On a clear, dark night, the Milky Way looks like a hazy band across the sky. That band is part of our galaxy’s disk seen from within.

When we look along the disk, stars at many different distances crowd into the same field of view, and dust obscures much of the light coming from the center.

Astronomers have used infrared telescopes such as Spitzer to look through some of that dust and trace the distribution of stars.

Those observations helped establish that our galaxy has a central bar. A face-on view of NGC 4394 makes it easier to picture how such a feature fits into a spiral galaxy.

The angle also makes it easier to follow the dust. In Hubble’s image, narrow dark filaments arc around the core and wind through the disk.

They stand out where they block light from the stars behind them. Farther along the arms, blue and pink knots punctuate the softer glow of the surrounding stars.

A bar may look like a solid feature in a still image, but the stars that make it up are moving around the galaxy.

One way a bar can form is when nearly circular stellar orbits become stretched. If enough of those elongated orbits line up, the combined light from the stars takes on the shape of a bar.

A passing galaxy can disturb a disk through gravity and help set that process in motion. A disk can also become unstable through gravitational interactions among its own stars.

Either way, a feature that spans a large part of the galaxy can emerge from changes in the paths of individual stars.

Once a bar forms, its gravity can help channel gas inward. That matters because gas supplies the raw material for new stars.

A bar can therefore influence where a galaxy builds its next generation of stars, even though the bright feature we see in the image is mostly the light of stars already there.

Hubble first captured NGC 4394 while studying a different galaxy. One instrument was trained on nearby Messier 85 and its star clusters, while another recorded an adjacent patch of sky containing NGC 4394.

Hubble’s team released that earlier image about a decade ago.

The new portrait combines those observations with data from a program studying 40 galaxies. NGC 4394 belongs to the Virgo Cluster, a gathering of more than 1,000 galaxies.

The researchers want to understand how star formation winds down in crowded environments and whether it follows a different course in galaxies with fewer neighbors.

Star clusters give researchers a way to look backward. By comparing how brightly a cluster shines at different wavelengths, astronomers can estimate its age.

A young cluster marks a place where stars formed relatively recently. Older clusters preserve evidence of earlier activity.

Taken together, their ages and locations can help researchers reconstruct where star formation persisted and where it faded.

That gives the specks along the spiral arms a second role in the image. The bar is the feature you can pick out at a glance, and it offers an immediate point of comparison with the Milky Way.

The star clusters are harder to spot. Each one carries a piece of the galaxy’s history, and Hubble can pick them out even though their light has crossed 55 million years of space to reach us.

#6321. Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

#6319. What helps land recover after fire? This ecologist looks to the past

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, asks how changes in the way people care for the land may have left it more vulnerable to wildfire.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

“My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”

#6318. Forest birds get more warning about predators when many other bird species live nearby

More bird species meant more alarm calls when a model hawk flew past, and recordings of more species drew bigger crowds of mobbing birds.

When an owl shows up in a forest during daylight hours, the small birds that see it make lots of noise. They gather around the owl and chirp out their calls. Almost immediately, birds of other species hear the calls and come to join the outcry.

A new study of forest birds in eastern China found more of these interspecies callings in places with greater bird species diversity. Joining forces allowed them to make more calls per minute, alerting everyone within earshot of the owl’s presence.

The result suggests that birds in forests that have fewer species may get less predator warnings, leaving them more vulnerable.

Two doctoral students, Agnishikhe Kumar and Jiahao Wu, are the study’s first authors. Both are at Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University in Suzhou, China, and the University of Liverpool.

Kumar and Wu worked with Eben Goodale, the study’s senior author, and with colleagues at Zhejiang University and other institutions in China, France, and the United States. All of the fieldwork took place in forest reserves in China.

Over more than two years, the team worked in ten nature reserves spread along about 1,025 miles (1,650 kilometers) of eastern China, from tropical Hainan to temperate Shaanxi.

Birds make two different kinds of calls about predators. Alarm calls go out when a predator is moving and attacking, and they often send the birds in a flock scattering into thick vegetation.

Mobbing calls are for a predator that isn’t moving, like an owl in daylight. These calls draw other birds toward the caller, and the crowd harasses the predator and can drive it away.

To set off alarm calls, the researchers used a slingshot to fire an 8-inch (20-centimeter) plastic hawk into the air beside mixed flocks of several species.

For mobbing, they put out a painted foam model of a collared owlet, a small owl that can attack birds, and played recordings of its calls.

Each time, they recorded how many species called, how many calls came per minute, and how quickly the first call came. They also measured the range of pitch the calls covered.

In an interview with Earth.com, Goodale credited his two students with the fieldwork. “Yeah, this was a ton of work,” he said. By his count, the total was 1,277 experiments.

Before each owl test, the team counted the bird species at the site. Where they counted more species, more kinds of birds joined the mobbing and more individual birds took part.

The birds at those sites also called at a higher rate, and their calls covered a wider range of pitch.

Pitch range matters because birds respond most to calls of other species that sound like their own. A broader mix of calls should reach more kinds of listeners.

On 41 islands in Thousand Island Lake, a reservoir in Zhejiang Province, the team saw a similar pattern. The number of bird species on those islands goes up with the size of the island.

Alarm calls were far rarer than mobbing calls. The plastic hawk set them off in 79 of 150 flocks.

The flocks that called gave a median of four alarm calls a minute, compared with a median of 52 calls a minute in the owl tests. One highly social species, Huet’s fulvetta, made 60.2% of all the alarm calls.

A bird that calls while a hawk is near may put itself at risk. Goodale told Earth.com the team thought the pattern might not hold for alarm calls, reasoning that “after one species calls, everyone else should eavesdrop on that and remain quiet.”

Instead, in flocks with more species, more kinds of birds gave alarm calls. The calls came at a higher rate and covered a wider range of pitch.

“We think it may be because the initial information may not be reliable,” Goodale said. Other species may need to keep calling, he added, to stress the threat and make sure the warning reaches their own kind.

In Sri Lanka, the authors wrote, the first bird to call in a flock is usually a babbler. That babbler often calls at any large or fast-moving bird, so the later calls of other species help mark a real attack.

The team found no significant link between a flock’s species count and how quickly the first alarm call came.

The hawk and owl tests showed how much calling went on. To learn whether birds of other species made use of it, the team ran an experiment at seven sites on the largest island in the lake.

Through two speakers, the researchers played the mobbing calls of one, two, four, or eight local species and recorded which birds responded. A recording of crickets, played to check that birds weren’t simply reacting to noise, drew no response.

Across 406 trials, recordings with more species drew more kinds of birds and more individuals. The birds that came made more calls, across a wider range of pitch. The increase leveled off as the number of species in the recording went up.

Birds of species that weren’t in the recording were also more likely to call within the first minute when the recording held more species. When the team counted all responding birds together, the first-minute pattern was too weak to rule out chance.

Huet’s fulvetta leads the mixed flocks in the region and often starts the mobbing. Goodale said the team expected it to play an outsized role in spreading information.

The experiment showed little sign of that. The team compared recordings of four species with and without each of the eight birds, across five measures.

In only four of those 40 comparisons was the response stronger when a particular species was included, and the four involved four different species.

All eight species drew relatively similar responses, Goodale said. “It seems birds are responding to the small acoustic differences between species and registering a higher response when they hear more species,” he added.

To test that idea, the team had built each recording two ways. In one version, every recording had 104 calls per minute, however many species were in it. In the other, each species called at its usual rate, so more species meant more calls.

Birds responded more to recordings with more species even when the number of calls stayed the same. The researchers took that as evidence that the variety of calls matters.

On most of the five measures, adding species had a stronger effect when the number of calls rose too. So the amount of calling appears to matter as well.

Goodale said the finding also applies in reverse. In areas with fewer animals because of habitat loss, hunting, or other causes, the animals that remain could be less informed.

Or they could come to rely more on collecting information themselves. When the information is about predators, he said, that could come at great cost.

The authors compared their finding to earlier studies that tied species diversity to pollination, seed dispersal, and pest control, and wrote that it helps justify conservation.

The experiments recorded how birds called and gathered, so they can’t show whether birds in places with more species are caught by predators less often.

Only mobbing calls were tested with recordings, and only on a single island. Earlier experiments elsewhere, which mostly compared one species with two, found weak effects on communication or no difference in response.

The larger scale of this study partly explains its stronger result, the authors wrote.

The same idea could apply to other information, such as where to find food or habitat, and to other animals. The researchers suggested that experiments with the chemical signals of insects and other invertebrates may be particularly useful.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Biology.

A recent satellite image captured a striking scene at the Shiveluch volcano, which has been erupting for nearly 30 years in Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Shiveluch volcano, Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia [56.66230841, 161.3449064]

What's in the photo? Snow melting around a growing lava dome at the volcano's summit

Which satellite took the photo? Landsat 9

This striking satellite snap shows a heavy blanket of snow surrounding a growing lava dome at the summit of one of Russia's most active and unstable volcanoes.

The snow-covered peak, called Shiveluch (also spelled Shivelyuch or Sheveluch), is a 10,771-foot-tall (3,283 meters) stratovolcano. The name Shiveluch loosely translates to "smoking mountain" in the language of the region's Indigenous Itelmen people. It is the northernmost active peak in the Kamchatka Peninsula, a highly volcanic region in eastern Russia that's famous for its unusually powerful and dramatically beautiful eruptions.

Shiveluch stands out even among its extremely active volcanic neighbors and is one of the planet's most active volcanoes, according to NASA's Earth Observatory. It has experienced at least 15 eruptions in the past 100 years, the most recent of which has been going on since 1999, according to the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program.

On average, the volcano spews around 530 million cubic feet (15 million cubic meters) of lava every year — enough to fill 6,000 Olympic-size swimming pools, according to a 2007 study. As a result, its appearance constantly changes when viewed from above.

"On a near-daily basis, satellites detect new signs of activity within [Shiveluch's] horseshoe-shaped caldera, including thermal anomalies, hot avalanches and debris flows," Earth Observatory representatives wrote. The volcano is also constantly spitting out "ash deposits that darken the surrounding landscape," they added.

A massive lava dome was growing from Shiveluch's summit. It likely looked something like this dome, which grew from the same place in 1993.

In this image, you might be able to see a particularly dark circle at the top of the volcano's caldera. This is a lava dome — a steep-sided landform that emerges when lava piles up on top of a volcanic vent — that has been growing rapidly in recent months, according to the Earth Observatory.

The lava within this swelling blob is "extruded slowly and piles up into lobed, sloped, or spine-like shapes akin to those that form when toothpaste is squeezed from a tube," Earth Observatory representatives wrote.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Eventually, lava domes grow so large that they give way under their own weight, often causing the caldera's walls to collapse. However, it doesn't take long for the volcano to rebuild itself after these events. (It is currently unclear if the photographed lava dome subsequently collapsed after the photo was taken.)

"Shivelyuch is an incredible volcano that has collapsed over and over again, on several scales, ranging from enormous flank collapses to more modest dome-collapse events," Janine Krippner, a volcanologist based in New Zealand, told the Earth Observatory. "It goes through cycles of collapse but then builds itself up again and again through constant volcanic activity."

Lava flows, visible as black lines snaking down the volcano's slopes and large patches of ash (at the bottom of the image) have retained so much heat that snow cannot settle on them, despite being months or even years old.

In a zoomed-out version of the satellite image (see above), black streaks are visible at various points along the volcano's flanks, including a thick dark line emanating from the summit caldera. These are lava flows from recent months or years that have retained enough heat that any snow that lands on them soon melts away, according to Live Science's sister site Space.com.

Krippner noted that when she previously visited Shiveluch for fieldwork, she could still feel heat coming from lava flows that were over 5 years old.

Further afield, you can also see larger black streaks that look as if they have been painted onto the satellite image with rough brushstrokes. These are patches of pyroclastic ash left over from a 2023 eruption that burned down large parts of a nearby forest, according to the Earth Observatory.

A 2022 astronaut photo shows a thick blanket of snow covering Yellowstone Lake, transforming the frozen body of water into a featureless white void. But below the ice lie some of Earth's hottest hydrothermal vents.

A 2025 satellite image shows a series of ghostly ice swirls sculpted on the surface of Lake Michigan by strong winds during an extreme cold snap that covered Chicago in a blanket of snow.

A 2017 astronaut photo shows an unusual checkered pattern surrounding a river, just south of the Canadian border. The unique sight is the result of a forest management initiative dating to the 1800s.
