#6217. Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life

Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.

Like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.

I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.

Being such a big city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.

In this post, I’ll help you plan an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

This first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.

The route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.

Just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.

After museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.

After a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.

Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.

In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.

The second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. Kilometer Zero is the official starting point of all the highways and railways in the country, making this effectively the center of the entire country. There’s a small plaque you can snap a photo of.

Nearby is the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue (El Oso y el Madroño). The statue shows a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).

From here, walk toward the iconic Plaza Mayor, highlighting its porticoed architecture and the Casa de la Panadería. Plaza Mayor once hosted bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments, and even executions. Now it’s ringed with tourist shops, cafés, and restaurants. It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.

For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.

After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. The largest palace in Western Europe, the Baroque-style palace was built in the 18th century and is home to over 3,400 lavishly decorated rooms. It was originally built on a former 9th-century Muslim fort and today functions much like an art museum with numerous works, including pieces by Caravaggio, Juan de Flandes, and Francisco Goya. Though it’s the official residence of the royal family, they don’t actually live here anymore, and the palace is only used for official state functions. You can walk through the palace (both self-guided and guided tours are available), starting at the grand stairway, and wander through lavishly decorated staterooms. There’s also the Royal Armory, which houses a collection of medieval weapons and armor.

To end the day, head to the Almudena Cathedral. Unlike many of the famous medieval churches in Europe, this one was constructed in the late 19th century. It was finally completed in 1993 and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II. While the exterior has a Neo-Classical design (to match the nearby palace), the cathedral also has a Neo-Romanesque crypt with over 400 columns that you can explore. Be sure to head up to the dome for stunning views out over the city.

Madrid is a paradise for foodies. It’s one of the reasons I keep coming back. While there are plenty of food tours to take in Madrid, I suggest heading off on your own to explore. Begin at the city’s iconic gastronomic markets. The glass-walled Mercado de San Miguel is a must for gourmet tapas near Plaza Mayor. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. Additionally, local favorites like Mercado de San Antón in Chueca and Mercado de Vallehermoso offer a deeper dive into regional flavors. Just make sure to bring an appetite.

If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.

For dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.

As the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.

For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.

Madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.

One popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.

Another option for a day trip is the Royal Palace and Gardens of Aranjuez, a World Heritage Cultural Landscape that rivals the beauty of Versailles. Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.

Lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).

On your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.

The Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. Over the years, this turned the convent into a veritable treasure trove of art.

The Royal Monastery of La Encarnación was founded in 1611 by the wife of Philip III, Margaret of Austria. It was a royal convent, meaning it had the direct support of the monarchy. While the exterior has an austere Baroque style, the interior is quite lavish, with ornate chapels, colorful frescoes, and lots of religious sculptures and paintings. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial said to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).

To end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.

While Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

#6216. Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

#6214. Faye Travel Insurance: The Best New Company Out there

We may receive compensation from Faye as an advertising partner. However, this does not influence our evaluations. Our opinions are our own.

I’ve been writing about travel for nearly two decades and, in that time, I’ve watched the travel insurance industry change at roughly the speed of a glacier. For years, the pitch was always the same: buy a policy, hope you never need it, and if something goes wrong, prepare for a paperwork marathon and a check that arrives somewhere between “eventually” and “you’ve forgotten you ever filed.”

I’ve personally been on the receiving end of that runaround. So have most travelers I know. It’s just something you kind of deal with. After all, you should never, ever, ever, EVER travel without travel insurance. You don’t want to end up needing a GoFundMe to pay your bills and get home if something goes wrong. (You can’t predict the future!)

Now, there’s a lot of players in this space but one I want to highlight today is Faye Travel Insurance, which I think is doing something unique.

Faye is a digital-first travel insurance company that launched coverage in the U.S. in 2022 so it’s pretty new to the US market when you consider that brands like World Nomads or Allianz have been offering coverage for over twenty years.

Faye is based on a pretty simple idea: travel insurance shouldn’t just sit there waiting for things to go wrong. It should actively help things go right.

That means whole-trip protection (your trip, your health, your stuff, even your pet), an app that’s actually useful while you’re traveling, 24/7 access to real human customer support, claims that get processed in days instead of months, and a digital wallet that pays you back almost instantly instead of waiting around for a check in the mail, which some companies still do in this day and age.

Faye has one plan for domestic and international trips, which makes things super easy. A lot of travel insurance companies have lots of plans and you end up squinting at coverage tables trying to figure out which one isn’t going to leave you stranded and has the coverage minimums you need. Faye built a single comprehensive plan that covers most of what travelers actually need:

These limits are pretty standard, especially on the medical coverage. If you want to add stuff on, they have a few optional addons that I think are really good and unique:

The CFAR insurance is really useful and I’ve rarely seen a company allow you to add it on to a policy. Usually, it’s already incorporated at a higher fee but this creates an affordable add on. I also love the pet care add on as more and more people travel with their pets.

Here’s where Faye really separates itself. Faye built something completely different! Here’s what you can actually do inside the Faye app:

Buy a policy in as little as 60 seconds – Plug in your trip details, get a quote, get covered.

Get real-time flight tracking and alerts – You’ll get delay info, gate changes, or baggage carousel numbers when you land! A lot of apps do this but this is a nice add on.

Telemedicine – Faye gives you access to a network of 20,000 telemedicine doctors in 21 languages when you travel abroad. If you wake up with food poisoning in a town where you don’t speak the language and don’t trust the local hospital reviews, you can talk to a doctor from your hotel bed. (As someone who has had to find doctors in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Find a doctor, pharmacy, ER, or ATM nearby – The app does the work of figuring out where to go when you’re disoriented and just need to find the closest open pharmacy at 11 p.m. in a city you arrived in five hours ago. (As someone who has had to do this in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Get free airport lounge access – If your flight is delayed by three hours or more, Faye gets you into a lounge – and who wouldn’t want lounge access with free food and drinks for a long delay?

Store your documents in Safekeeping – Securely u     pload your passport, visa, insurance card, vaccination records. If anything gets lost or stolen, you’ve got digital copies.

Check destination essentials before you go – Visa requirements, plug adapter types, local emergency numbers, weather, currency conversion, even local apps worth downloading.

Chat with real humans, 24/7 – Actual customer experience specialists, available every day of the year, including weekends and holidays.

Buy an eSIM – The app also enables you to purchase an eSIM meaning you can avoid pesky physical SIM swaps and get connected to the internet right when you land.

Here’s how Faye works: something bad happens. You open the app. You file a claim in a few minutes by uploading photos of your receipts. If it’s a qualifying issue like a baggage delay or flight delay, you may get reimbursed almost instantly. Funds go straight into Faye Wallet, a digital payment card built into the app that connects to Apple Pay or Google Pay. You tap and pay, right then and there, for whatever you actually need: a new outfit, toiletries, dinner, a hotel.

For larger or more complex claims, Faye aims to resolve them within 48 hours. of receiving the necessary documentation.

If you don’t want to use the digital wallet, you can transfer the funds to your bank account or get a paper check.

Pricing depends on your trip cost, destination, length, state of residence and age (same as every insurance product) but prices start at around $5.16 a day for international trips, which is a lot more competitive than other companies out there.

I’ve used a lot of travel insurance companies over the years. Most of them are fine. A few are awful. Faye is the first one that feels like it was designed by people who actually understand modern travel and get that we’re booking trips on our phones, communicating in apps, and expecting the same digital convenience from insurance that we get from everything else.

The combination of whole-trip protection, the app, Faye Wallet, real human support, and fast claims has genuinely changed how I think about this category. Travel insurance used to be the thing I bought and forgot.

If you’re heading out on a trip soon, check it out at withfaye.com, get a quote, and see for yourself.

#6213. Don’t Scan This Abroad: The QR Code Travel Scam Tourists Miss

QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them

A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

From a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real company.

You think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

You may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

If anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

That does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

The FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

Do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

If the message says you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

We call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the company, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that include a QR code and pressure people to pay a fake unpaid balance.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

Open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car company, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

First, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

If you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car company, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

A QR code may be suspicious if it looks like a sticker placed over another code, has peeling edges, opens a strange URL, uses a shortened link, creates urgency, asks for information that does not make sense, or directs you away from the official website or app.

At a restaurant, a QR menu should not need your passport or banking password. At a parking meter, the payment page should match the city or parking authority. At a hotel, a check-in code should not send you to a random payment page outside the official booking system.

The BBB has also warned consumers to double-check QR codes before paying for parking.

No. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

The goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

Before scanning a public QR code at a restaurant, parking meter, hotel, airport, train station, attraction, or transit stop, remember the rule:

Inspect the code. Read the link. Go directly to the official website or app when money, passwords, or personal information are involved.

That tiny pause may be the thing that saves your trip.

Scanning a QR code is not automatically dangerous. The danger usually begins when you open a suspicious page, enter payment details, type a password, download a file, or provide personal information without checking whether the site is legitimate.

Inspect the physical code for stickers, raised edges, bubbles, peeling corners, or anything placed over another code. Then check the URL preview before opening the page. If the link looks strange or does not match the official company, city, hotel, or attraction, do not use it.

Before entering payment information, make sure the website belongs to the official business or authority. When in doubt, use the official app, type the website manually, pay directly at the machine, or ask staff for the correct payment method.

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the official number on the back of your card or your banking app. Watch for suspicious charges, replace the card if needed, and do not use any contact information from the suspicious website.

#6212. Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

#6211. Nomad Citizen: A New Social Safety Net for Entrepreneurs

If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health plan, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

The travel insurance company Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just launched what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

Nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single plan. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

Nomad Citizen covers people under 56 and earning at least $4,000 USD per month. You sign up online, choose your start date, declare that you’re in good health, and confirm you’ll be outside your passport country for more than half the year. You can also add your partner and any children under 18.

But who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really quickly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

For those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the plan can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

Income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

If you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

Health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage: Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance,  you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support: You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

For health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking new income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This new Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

#6210. Holafly Plans: The Best eSIM Plan for Long Term Travelers

There are a lot of eSIM companies in the world. They all work a similar way: you download their app, pick your package, install the eSIM into your smartphone, and off you go. There’s many I like.

But one I like more than the rest is Holafly and I’ve been using their eSIMs for years. I find their app to be easy to use and their rates really competitive.

So when Holafly launched Holafly Plans, a single eSIM that works as an ongoing subscription across 160+ destinations, I was excited. It’s a great option for those who are looking for more data and flexibility than a traditional eSIM. (An eSIM is a digital SIM built directly into your phone’s hardware, so there’s no physical card to insert or swap. Instead of visiting a shop for a plastic SIM, you activate a plan by scanning a QR code or installing it through an app, and you’re connected within minutes. Because it’s software-based, a single phone can hold multiple eSIMs, letting you switch between a home number and a local or global travel plan without touching your device. I have like 10 installed. lol)

In this post, I’m going to explain what the product is, how it’s different than a traditional eSIM, and who I think this option is for!

Holafly Plans is a single global eSIM that covers more than 160 destinations on one ongoing subscription. You buy it once, install it once, and it just keeps working as you move from country to country. You don’t reswap SIMs, you don’t redownload anything, there’s no re-purchasing, and no hunting for a new QR code every time you land somewhere new.

It automatically reconnects you when you land in a new place. Think of it as like a traditional mobile carrier – but a lot cheaper.

You can buy it monthly or annually and it comes in two tiers: Light and Unlimited. There’s no annual contract and you can cancel any time.

The Unlimited Plan includes no data caps and an unlimited hotspot so you can tether your laptop on the go. If you’re a digital nomad uploading video, doing video calls, or just someone who doesn’t want to think about data ever again, this is a great add-on. This tier also comes with a local phone number from the US, UK, or Canada, which lets you receive SMS messages.

The Light Plan gives you 25GB of data a month, still includes a hotspot, and still covers the same 160+ destination coverage. For someone who mostly uses maps, messaging apps, and the occasional Instagram scroll, this package is probably the best option.

Additionally, with both Holafly Plans, once your plan is active, you get their “Always On” feature which is 1GB of backup data every month, automatically for life, even if you eventually cancel your subscription entirely.

Pricing varies a bit by region and currency and depending on how long you purchase, so check out their current rates on the Holafly Plans page. However, as an example, their unlimited plan is only $55 USD per month for 1 year, which is a lot cheaper than any US based carrier charges for their base option that includes unlimited 5G data overseas.  You can get monthly, quarterly, or yearly plans. Quarterly plans save approximately 10% while yearly plans save 15%.

Use the promo code NOMADICMATT at checkout to get 10% OFF Holafly Plans and 5% OFF all standard Holafly eSIMs.

Classic Holafly eSIMs are built for a single trip. You pick a country or region (there are 200+ available), choose how many days of data you need, and it covers just that trip. If you’re flying to Portugal for two weeks, a classic eSIM is still the simpler, cheaper option. It’s a one-and-done purchase. If you only take a couple trips per year then this is still the best option.

On the other hand, if you’re a digital nomad who is gone from your home country most of the year and moving between different countries all the time, then the Holafly Plans fly is the much better option. It’s a standing global subscription designed for people who are more or less always somewhere. Instead of buying a new eSIM every time your itinerary changes, you have one number, one connection, one bill that follows you across borders indefinitely. #6209. Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

#6208. Mother Says Delta Seated Her Toddler Separately And Told Her To Ask Other Passengers To Move

A mother says Delta Air Lines separated her from her two-year-old daughter, then told her to ask other passengers to switch seats. She says she had purchased Comfort+ and originally selected seats together. If her account is accurate, this was a problem for Delta to resolve before boarding, not something to leave a parent negotiating in the aisle.

In a Reddit post, a passenger describes trying to resolve separate seat assignments on a flight from Orlando (MCO) to Atlanta (ATL). She was traveling with her husband, their 2½-year-old daughter, and their one-year-old son.

She says she was directed to the gate for assistance, but received this response:

“I explained that she’s two and cannot sit by herself. Their solution? Tell me it was my responsibility to ask other passengers to switch seats.”

When commenters questioned whether she had purchased basic economy or failed to select seats, she clarified that she had booked Comfort+. After checking her original confirmation, she added:

“I just looked and it was definitely Delta. I have 3 flight / time changes – I originally booked us in 15 D / 15 E / 15 F – we ended up in 15 F / 15 A / 16 A.”

This remains her account and we don’t have a way to verify the booking history or the exchange with the gate staff. She also does not clearly state how the family ultimately sat onboard.

I have traveled extensively with my children, including when they were very young. There is a considerable difference between wanting the entire family together and needing a two-year-old beside a parent.

It is unreasonable to ask an airline to rearrange a cabin so that every adult in a traveling party can sit together. Heidi and I can sit apart. One parent can sit with one child while the other sits elsewhere with the other child. We have done that many times.

But a toddler needs an adult who can help with the seatbelt, food, and everything else that comes with flying at that age. The stranger assigned to the adjacent seat cannot reasonably become the person expected to provide that help.

I see no excuse for the Delta agent. Once an agent knows a toddler has been assigned a seat away from both parents, someone needs to take responsibility for finding a workable arrangement and it should be someone in a position of authority…like the gate agent.

I am also sympathetic to passengers who pre-select a seat and then find themselves pressured to move.

A parent should not board, occupy someone else’s seat, and announce that the family needs to sit together and a passenger should not be shamed for declining an aisle-to-middle swap. There may be very good reasons that person selected that particular seat, and those reasons are not necessarily anyone else’s business.

That is precisely why the airline should handle this.

An agent can review the seat map, identify possible swaps, and ask for volunteers. If necessary, the airline can offer an incentive rather than expect a stranger to absorb the inconvenience for free. There may also be a solution involving a different cabin, provided the family agrees and any fare difference is addressed.

The ultimate solution to situations like these does not have to preserve every preference the family had when booking. It does need to put a young child beside a responsible adult.

The published Delta family seating policy states:

“Delta strives to seat family members together upon request.”

It directs customers who cannot obtain seats together online or through the app to contact reservations to review the available options. That wording is less reassuring than a guarantee. Even so, I would expect the assistance to amount to more than telling a parent to start asking around once onboard.

Parents should understand fare restrictions and select seats when possible, but a two-year-old’s need to sit beside a parent does not disappear because the family purchased a cheaper ticket and it becomes legally dicey to not sell basic economy tickets to young children. However, in this case it was not a basic economy ticket but a Comfort+ seat.

Selecting seats months in advance does not mean you can stop checking them. Whenever I receive a schedule change, I review the flights and seat assignments and check again often in the week leading up to travel. Be sure to take a screenshot of your original seat assignments if they were not reflected on your ticket confirmation.

If a young child becomes separated from a parent, contact the airline promptly and explain the child’s age. If reservations cannot resolve it, arrive early and ask an airport agent…don’t agree to negotiate onboard…it’s unreasonable, even for Frontier Airlines.

This is called “gardening” your reservation.

A mother says Delta assigned her toddler a separate seat and left her to ask other passengers to move, despite originally booking seats together in Comfort+. We have only her account, but the underlying expectation is reasonable: a two-year-old should sit beside a parent, and the airline should help arrange that.

Other passengers deserve respect for their seat choices too. Resolving the issue before boarding protects everyone from an awkward confrontation that should never have been necessary…

#6207. Airline Elite Status So Close, Yet So Far: The Drawback To Being A Free Agent

I boast often about being a free agent when it comes to both hotels and airlines…I’m done chasing elite status (at least top-tier elite status) because the cost/benefit analysis no longer works for me. But there are some days I wonder…

I fly United quite a bit and if I’m being honest, the experience is usually excellent…I seek out the A321neo, as Starlink has shifted from a nice bonus to requirement. But it’s not just that. The food has improved and service has been great..flight attendants appear happy (they have a contract after all) and the operation has also been good: my personal on-time arrival rate with United is over 90% while it hovers at around 50% for American.

And sometimes after another great United flight, like my journey back to California over the weekend, I do wonder if I  am better served just getting back on the hamster wheel and putting most of my eggs in the United basket. This flight was from Chicago to Los Angeles and I just missed the upgrade to first class as a Gold…had I been Platinum, I would have scored an upgrade.

I’m close…not that I’m projected to spend $5K in the last month of the year on United airfare…but it is conceivably within reach. And in the next month I’m flying Aer Lingus, American, Delta, JetBlue, KLM, and United….maybe even more.

And having Premier Platinum status would certainly help with some upgrades and I’d put the PlusPoints to use…

But then I pinch myself and think I’m actually only 2/3 there with 1/12 of the year left…and to spend all that money on United instead of flying the carriers and routings and times that work best for me (mostly in premium cabins…) just doesn’t make sense.

So I return to reality and think, no, the status just isn’t worth it and if I really need the premium cabin seat, I’ll pay for it. And the irony is that the majority of my flights this year have been in premium cabins and to reach top-tier status you have to essentially buy premium cabin fares anyway or else you will never spend enough. So what’s the point? Free baggage? Extra legroom seats for the family? I don’t find that worthwhile.

So I guess the bottom line is that by splitting my loyalty this year I’ll make Gold on American and Gold on United (nothing on Alaska, Delta, or JetBlue, though I have flown them all) whereas I could have rather easily made Platinum on United had I been a bit more loyal to a product that I do genuinely like.

But no. I still think I’m making the correct choice for my circumstances.

And yet it’s the allure of frequent flyer elite status is still somewhat enchanting…

#6205. Delta Teases Seattle Longhaul Announcement And Singapore Flights Look Like A Safe Bet

Delta Air Lines appears to be preparing another Asia announcement, with a Seattle event next month fueling speculation about a new nonstop flight to Singapore. That would fit what Delta executives have already said about returning to the city-state, though the airline has not yet confirmed a Seattle–Singapore launch date or schedule.

An invitation circulating on reddit promotes a “Delta Night Market” at Seattle’s Museum of Pop Culture. Travelers are interpreting the event as a potential setting for an Asia-Pacific route announcement. What makes Singapore more than a random guess is that Delta has already said it intends to return.

Even aviation insider Jon NYC is convinced:

In an August interview with The Points Guy, Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito said:

In that interview, Esposito ruled out Los Angeles as the departure point, making Seattle the obvious candidate among Delta’s West Coast hubs. Recall that a Delta presentation hosted on the FAA website, prepared for a July Pacific air traffic coordination meeting, listed Manila and Singapore as new markets for 2027.

So while we may not have a Seattle–Singapore timetable yet, I think it is very safe to say the announcement is coming very soon.

Delta would not be creating a new nonstop market. Singapore Airlines already connects Seattle and Singapore with Airbus A350-900 service.

But another operator would give passengers more choice, and Delta could draw connecting traffic from its domestic network in addition to travelers beginning or ending their journeys in Seattle: competition that I always welcome.

Singapore Airlines is a formidable carrier, but having another nonstop option could be useful even for passengers who ultimately continue choosing Singapore Airlines.

This would fit a broader investment in Seattle. Delta has already announced daily Seattle–Tokyo Narita service beginning March 27, 2027, operated by an Airbus A330-900neo. That flight will complement its existing Haneda service.

It also added Barcelona and Rome from Seattle this year. While I view this expansion as a tit-for-tat with Alaska Alines (a battle I’m not sure Delta is going to win), I welcome it nonetheless…I don’t really care why Delta or Alaska add more route: they are good for consumers, even if they only last a couple of seasons.

For whatever the reason, I appreciate seeing Delta expand its own longhaul network. Its partnerships are useful, but there is value in offering passengers a nonstop flight on its own aircraft rather than requiring a connection through a partner hub…and I can’t wait to try the new Delta One soft product.

For Seattle travelers, the growing competition is especially welcome. I care less about which airline gets to call itself the city’s global carrier than whether passengers have useful schedules, competitive fares, and more places they can reach without changing planes.

A Delta event in Seattle has renewed speculation about nonstop Singapore service. Singapore looks like the leading contender because Delta has already committed publicly to returning, and Seattle fits the information executives have shared…I’m comfortable enough to say with very high certainty that a SEA-SIN announcement is coming shortly.

LAX-ICN is still very likely the next route that DL will add making yet another unique market that it serves among US carriers. LAX-MNL will be unique among US carriers for DL as ICN will likely be as well.

DL’s cadence of a new TPAC route start every 6 months is likely to continue for years into the future.

Is anybody really going to SIN. I say that somewhat ironically because I’m literally flying there tonight, but what is the actual daily O/D traffic between SEA and SIN? It isn’t HK, JP, CN, or KR.

There are so so many other one stop routings from basically every city in the US that are better than flying Delta in every single way. This just seems so unnecessary. Honestly, BKK seems to me like it would be more viable.

Singapore will out-yield Bangkok every day. The Thais aren’t in the same league.

#6204. Masked ICE Agents Arrest Father And Daughter Boarding Alaska Airlines Flight, But “Visa Overstay” Is Not The Whole Story

ICE arrested a father and daughter as they boarded an Alaska Airlines flight in Seattle, and the government’s explanation is that they overstayed their visas. But their attorney says they entered legally, have pending immigration applications and valid work permits, and have no criminal history. I support secure borders…but I think this operation deserves a better explanation than “they broke the law.”

By now, you may have seen the disturbing passenger recordings from the jet bridge for Alaska Airlines flight 1306 from Seattle to Los Angeles on November 21, 2026.

Masked federal officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and his adult daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, during boarding. The encounter involved a struggle in front of other passengers and delayed the flight.

Masked ICE agents detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as passengers were boarding a flight. Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave them no advance notice of the operation. pic.twitter.com/r44WPTvGdv

— Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) November 22, 2026

The crew was so shaken by the incident that replacements had to be called in, delaying the flight for three hours.

Yesterday, the family’s attorney, Olia Catala, claimed they were traveling to California for a family baptism.

ICE says Mendoza overstayed his visa. It also alleges that Hernandez Mejia threw hot coffee at officers during the encounter and says she could face an assault charge.

On November 21, 2026, at approximately 8:05 a.m. PST, ICE officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an illegal alien from Mexico who overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws.

During the arrest other travelers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers—a federal crime and a felony. One passenger hurled hot coffee on the officers. Other passengers began obstructing federal officers.

The individual who threw the hot coffee was identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, an illegal alien from Mexico and visa overstay. She was subsequently arrested as well. She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime and a felony. Secretary Mullin has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the fullest extent of the law. Our brave law enforcement is facing more than a 1,600% increase in assaults, 3,300% increase in vehicular attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats against them. This violence must end.

On November 21, 2026, at approximately 8:05 a.m. PST, ICE officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an illegal alien from Mexico who overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws.

During the arrest other travelers began to… https://t.co/nXiBxAqIJ5

— U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (@ICEgov) November 22, 2026

The family’s lawyer disputes that account, saying the coffee spilled during the confrontation. An eyewitness has also challenged the government’s description. If Mejia did deliberately throw coffee on officers, she should be held accountable.

The family’s account adds information that is critical to this discussion.

Catala says the father and daughter entered the United States legally in 2015 and subsequently sought asylum. The father’s application remains pending. The daughter has since married a U.S. citizen and has a separate application to adjust her immigration status. According to their attorney, both have work authorization and neither has a criminal record.

Yes, a work permit is not a Green Card and a pending immigration application does not automatically prevent detention: I am not declaring that ICE lacked legal authority to make these arrests.

Even so, if the government permits someone to work while it considers an immigration application, the expiration of the original tourist admission does not tell us everything we need to know about that person’s circumstances.

We constantly hear that people should come legally and follow the process. Here, the family’s lawyer says they entered legally and have been pursuing that process for years. I’m not seeing any information to justify the raid in hte DHS statement above…I struggle to understand the urgency of arresting these particular travelers on the way to a family baptism.

And sorry, but I don’t think federal agents should be allowed to wear masks. Here it may have violated Washington State law, but it is more fundamental: the masks betray fear…not reasonable fear of crazy people attacking them for doing their jobs…but subconscious fear that they pursuing injustice, not justice, and that there is often a difference between the spirit of the law and the letter of the law.

I hope that President Trump and the Democratic-controlled Congress can reach a grand bargain on immigration reform. Give Trump his wall if it means a pathway to citizenship for those otherwise law-abiding citizens who may have entered illegally but are now part of the American fabric. Let’s make a deal.

Alaska Airlines published its statement on Saturday afternoon, complaining it was not given notice of the immigration raid:

“In this instance, Alaska Airlines was not provided appropriate notice of the enforcement action.”

The airline says it must comply with applicable law, but does not direct or coordinate immigration enforcement. It expressed concern for affected passengers and employees and said it would work with the Port of Seattle and government authorities to determine whether proper protocols were followed.

Alaska too is right to demand answers about an operation that disrupted boarding and left its employees managing the consequences.

The Port of Seattle’s initial statement opened:

“We are outraged about this morning’s incident involving ICE and two passengers as travelers boarded AS 1306 to Los Angeles.”

The Port said it did not participate in the enforcement action and was examining with DHS whether previously agreed airport protocols had been breached. On Monday, commissioners went further, calling for a review of airport access and security credentials. Commissioner Sam Cho said:

“The traveling public and our airport employees should not be left wondering whether they are witnessing a lawful arrest or an abduction. Period”

That concern strikes me as reasonable. Passengers should be able to identify law enforcement and understand what is happening around them, especially in a confined space immediately outside an aircraft.

Again and again I return to this: whether an agency has authority to act and whether it exercised that authority wisely are separate questions.

I know that interdicting illegal aliens make a lot sense in airports because it is easy to verify where someone is and relatively easy to detain them if you know what flight they will be boarding or arriving on. But on a crowded jetbridge?

A jet bridge is a narrow passageway with passengers carrying bags, sometimes holding children, and often standing in a line that barely moves. There is little room to step away when a confrontation begins.

I see abosutley no need to for these (yes, I see no need for these raids at all for visa overstays without criminal records). I also reject the idea that concern about these tactics means supporting open borders or opposing immigration enforcement. We can enforce immigration laws and still expect the government to exercise restraint and judgment.

For me, the unresolved coffee allegation reinforces the need for a careful review. Deliberately throwing hot coffee at officers would be serious (an accidental spill during a sudden struggle would be a very different matter). The available accounts conflict, and the consequences for the daughter could be substantial.

There should be an accounting of what occurred before the passenger recordings began, how officers identified themselves, and why this operation unfolded during boarding. I hope more recordings emerge.

The government says it arrested visa overstayers. Their lawyer says they have pending immigration applications, work permits, and no criminal history. Both seem to be true, which is precisely why the victory lap by DHS is an inadequate explanation.

I support enforcing immigration laws, but I want to understand why these travelers were targeted in this manner and whether the force used was justified. The GOP lost big in the Midterms because reasonable Americans who do support secure borders did not vote for this sort of nefarious tomfoolery. Alaska Airlines and airport officials deserve answers. So do the family and the passengers who found themselves caught in the middle. As I often ask, where are the adults in the room?

#6201. American Airlines Expands Block On Last-Minute Partner Award Bookings

American Airlines appears to have expanded a frustrating restriction on last-minute award travel. Domestic connections are now subject to the same six-day cutoff that already blocked nonstop saver awards through partner programs. For travelers using Alaska Atmos Rewards points or British Airways Avios, another useful way to book American flights seems to have vanished.

As first flagged by One Mile At A Time, American is now withholding saver award inventory on wholly domestic connecting itineraries within 144 hours of departure. The restriction affects both economy and premium cabins.

American began blocking domestic nonstop saver awards within that window in May. Connections initially remained available, but that appears to have changed. International itineraries, including those with domestic connections, reportedly remain outside this restriction.

When using AA miles, there appears to be no change. AAdvantage members can still book flights through American itself, where award prices vary. The restriction concerns the inventory that other frequent flyer programs need to sell an award on American.

First, a short primer…each day this blog has folks who have read it for almost 20 years and those who are reading it for the first time.

A seat available for miles on AA.com is not necessarily available to Alaska or British Airways. American controls what it releases to those programs, and its own award pricing varies by flight and date.

When the original restriction emerged, flights disappeared from partner searches as they crossed the six-day threshold, even while remaining available through AAdvantage.

So an empty search result on a partner website does not necessarily mean the flight is full or that American has stopped accepting miles. It may simply mean you have the wrong kind of miles…

I understand why American might prefer that someone book through AAdvantage rather than redeem another airline’s currency. Giving travelers a reason to accumulate its own miles has commercial value and is part of AA’s plan to return to profitability.

But understanding the incentive does not make this a welcome development.

One of the most useful things about miles is being able to arrange a trip when cash fares are high. Think family emergency or holiday travel.

In those circumstances, having access to American through another program can be very valuable. Removing that option makes the points already sitting in those accounts less useful, even if the published award chart does not change.

We spend plenty of time discussing award price increases, but availability deserves just as much attention. An attractive mileage price is of little practical value when the program cannot book the flight you need, which is frequent criticism of Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards, now even less valuable than due to AA blocking space.

No one is asking American to release every unsold seat to every partner….AA has every right to monetize as many seats as it can, just like it doing with first class upgrades.

Still, I would rather see American manage availability flight by flight than impose a broad cutoff based on how soon someone wants to travel. A flight with weak demand and a flight that is nearly sold out do not present the same commercial circumstances.

American does not comment on program changes like this, but has apparently concluded that the additional control is worth the lost partner bookings. Without knowing the reimbursement arrangements, I am not going to pretend I can calculate that trade-off.

From the passenger perspective, however, this is another reason to temper expectations about airline partnerships. The ability to earn points in one program and redeem them across a network is a major selling point. Restrictions like this make that promise less useful…and this is hardly a unique trend: we see the same thing with Delta and United.

If you need an American flight within six days of departure, check AAdvantage directly, for now that is your only option. Always compare the mileage price with the cash fare too…using miles is not automatically the better deal and is often not.

For travel farther out, I would still compare partner options before booking. But I would be certainly not transfer points speculatively while hoping that domestic American availability will open shortly before departure.

The expansion of partner award blocking removes another option for travelers hoping to use miles for last-minute domestic American flights. AAdvantage remains an option, but it’s a big blow to Alaska Airlines Atmos members.

I understand why American wants to favor its own program. Even so, I cannot celebrate this news.
