#6179. The Essential Cookbooks to Break Out Every Holiday Season

The holidays always bring about a flurry of travel, but even if you find yourself hosting in your own home this year, you can always explore new frontiers by way of a good cookbook. At Traveler, the titles we swear by take us through H Mart with an expert guide at hand to break down the aisles, to Sri Lanka, where the palette of London hot spot Hoppers was formed, and to the sugar-dusted counters of Broma Bakery, where Sarah Fennel has the key to 100 desserts sure to satisfy any sweet tooth. The best cookbooks immerse you in the corner of the world they come from, and through their pages, narrative transforms into a multi-sensory experience. Just as we're placing finishing touches on our holiday menus, our editors gathered their favorite cookbooks of all time that take readers all across the map, from recent releases that have become instant classics in our households to vintage volumes that continue to stand the test of time.

We'd love to hear about the cookbooks that take a place of pride in your kitchen on Instagram or Facebook.

I was lucky enough to taste chef Ifrah Ahmed's food at a beautiful dinner last year, so I couldn't wait to add her cookbook Soomaaliya to my shelf when it came out this spring. In Somalia, she writes, "knowledge is passed down orally," but she records the flavors and traditions of the culture in this stunning homage to Somalia's rich culinary legacy. —Sarah Khan, contributing editor

When I’m working my way through a recipe or just slapping something together for the sake of a pantry clean-out, odds are that the secret ingredient that ties it all together is an item I picked up at H Mart. Perhaps it’s the splash of Shaoxing cooking wine that makes all the notes in a fried rice sing that much more, or the half-packet of Buldak sauce that brings on the much-needed heat to some peanut noodles. As a card-carrying fan of the brand, I was ecstatic when I learned H Mart co-president Stacey Kwon had committed the splendor of the Korean grocery store’s aisles to pages in a cookbook. Beyond just housing recipes (the Galbi Jjim is a dinner party show-stopper), this omnibus also lets readers in on the store’s history, the tips and tricks of navigating its inventory, and handy guides that will have you cooking like it's second nature. This volume is a boon for H Mart enthusiasts and a fantastic tool for those just beginning their journey in the kitchen. —Kat Chen, editorial assistant, destinations

I love Hoppers, the dish. I love Hoppers, the homey London restaurant chain dishing out delicious Sri Lankan and southern Indian fare. So it’s a no-brainer that I love cooking from Hoppers, the cookbook. With the recipes in this book, author and restaurant owner Karan Gokani attempts to make traditional dishes like lamb kari and buriani feel approachable, all with the trademark come-join-me affability of his Instagram cooking videos. Some of these recipes are Proustian madeleines, taking me back to early-morning visits to fish markets in southern India or the many holidays spent along Sri Lanka’s southern coast, as well as to my grandmother’s dining table in Kerala. There’s a striking overlap in ingredients and flavors when it comes to Kerala and Sri Lanka, and it’s always a pleasure to get to sample that shared heritage. Now, if only I could summon a supply of the Arrack Attack cocktails from Hoppers as I cooked… —Arati Menon, global digital director

Since I’ve moved to New York, I’ve known that whenever I’m looking for a taste of home, I can always head to the East Village or Williamsburg to Taiwanese-American restaurant Win Son (and its bakery off-shoots). And now with the restaurant’s cookbook, I can recreate their lu rou fan (braised pork rice) or tsang ying tou (fly’s head, a fragrant mix of pork and chives that goes over rice) for myself. I’m fortunate to have grown up with a mom who was a fantastic cook, but the magic she worked in the kitchen has always been obscure to me. She’s true to the trope of never writing any recipes down, instead relying on muscle memory and years of road-tested intuition. But with the wisdom of Ku, Brown, and Erway’s book by my side, I’ve finally been able to master my childhood dishes and resist the urge to order takeout. —K.C.

I became interested in plant-based dining once I started dating a vegan, and one of the first restaurants that opened my eyes to all the possibilities of letting go of meat was Amanda Cohen’s Dirt Candy. It’s one of my favorite restaurants in the whole city, with a seasonal tasting menu that doesn’t break the bank but still stretches your imagination by showing you the full flavor spectrum of a leek, or proving by example that yes, eggplant really does belong in a dessert. Their cookbook is an absolute joy to read through, especially since it’s part comic book! It’s as fun as it is revelatory, and it’s a showcase of how cooking is an art as well as a form of play. —K.C.

A friend gifted me Table for Two when my partner and I moved in together a few years ago. It was sweet, and the cover added some much-needed color and beauty to my kitchen counter. But its not just a pretty face—this cookbook has challenged me. From slow-cooked lamb and cinnamon stew to fluffy, peach crepes, these recipes are made to impress. You’ll find a mix of one-pan meals, specialty dinners, delicious lunches, and rich desserts. If you’re trying to win someone over, this cookbook will help you every step of the way. —M.K.

When it comes to educational heroes, Alton Brown is on the pediment alongside Bill Nye and LeVar Burton for me. Watching his show Good Eats on Food Network was a formative ritual; he just has this infectious geekiness about him. As a sort of food mad scientist, Brown can be technical bordering on obsessive, but it’s that attention to detail that makes his methods so approachable: cooking is something you can break down to its basics and understand. This first volume is all about the fundamentals, and with it you’ll never make a bad batch of brownies or dry turkey again. —K.C.

I stumbled upon this vintage cookbook at a secondhand bookstore, and I initially purchased it as a novelty item. I’d never seen a cookbook dedicated to an appliance before, let alone one I had never associated with “cooking” to begin with. But much like how I’d imagine Methven’s initial readership reacted in 1978, I was pleasantly shocked and excited by how versatile the microwave really is. There are recipes ranging from Scallops Au Gratin to Barbecue Ribs to Seven-Minute Brownies in this book, and I’ve gleaned many staples from its pages. It’s only right to acknowledge you’re not going to get restaurant-quality versions or true-to-form authenticity out of every dish, but if you’re wiling to adventure, this is one of the most accessible ways to do it from your own home. Sometimes when I’m at a loss for what to make and feeling sluggish, I’ll perform a little bibliomancy on this book to figure out lunch. Even if you’re just interested in this title for your coffee table, the photography is beautiful and occasionally experimental in its efforts to display the science behind the new-fangled microwave. —K.C.

#6178. Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden said he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

It’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

The sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”

One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

“I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling showed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

#6176. On Location: Dig Stars Amy Poehler and Geraldine Viswanathan on Italian Gelato, Go-Karting—and Tailgating

On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we take a look at Dig.

Amy Poehler had never been to Greece, but she was immediately entranced by Kate Myers’s novel Excavations about four women coming together for an archaeological dig in Athens. So she took her first trip there to set the scene for her 10-part Peacock comedy series Dig, which drops November 23.

“The way in which Greek people mingle with real antiquities every day, walking past very important structures, is archaeology in process,” the Saturday Night Live alum tells Traveler. “The old and the new are constantly bumping up against each other. It was very cool to be there and really helped remind us of the theme of the show that the past is just around the corner and you can't hide from it.”

Each of the characters comes to the dig site at different stage of their life, with Poehler as an archaeologist stuck as second fiddle to beloved Neville (Hugh Laurie). But it’s her bond with fellow diggers, heartbroken free spirit Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), young and flustered Patty (Fina Strazza), and refined but ready to rebel Clare (Antonia Thomas) that provides the backbone of the series—a coming of age story for every age.

Despite being set purely in Greece, Poehler says they quickly found that “Puglia wine country, Greece, and Los Angeles can kind of double for each other, which is weird." So the team made southeastern Italy their home base, checking in at Rocco Forte's Masseria Torre Maizza, where they indulged in seafood (“We got overwhelmed by how good the food was!”) and bought tons of pottery wherever they traveled, a side effect of talking about it on the show so much.

Off-set, they found high-speed fun, thanks to the keen ears of Laurie. “We could hear the roar of go-karts from our hotel, so he went around on a motorbike—he's so cool—and found this place,” Viswanathan says of Circuit Kart Evolution in Fasano. Poehler jumps in: “The crew and most of the cast raced, but a couple of outsider Europeans who snuck in ended up winning because they had the real lead foot!”

Amy Poehler's 10-part Peacock series films all across the Mediterranean.

As for where a second season could take them, the cast will only drop hints. Viswanathan says it will be “a little spicier," while Poehler adds “it would be more passionate and fiery." But one thing's for sure, they are ready to start digging again soon. "We have some ideas for where to go and what kind of stuff we could dig up,” Poehler says. “Archeological digs are in a lot of different countries, so we could go all over!”

With her executive producer hat on, Poehler really honed in on the details of Greek culture during her time in Athens, in order to capture that same essence on screen. “I’m a New Yorker, so Athens is a really cool, vibrant, interesting city, but it does have a lot more graffiti than we expected,” she admits, adding that “some of it is really beautiful.” That meant they had to add that grittiness to some of their recreated sets in Italy and California. Another unique aspect: “the light in Greece is so specific and beautiful,” she says of the natural rays. The best part? “We got to wrap and then go have the best salad you’d ever had in your life—I’m still thinking about it.” Her favorite was a meal at Barbounaki, where “the guy basically said trust me and came back with a whole fish and cut it at the table—it was so good.”

The fifth-century BCE Temple of Poseidon serves as an epic ancient backdrop in Dig.

Just over an hour’s drive southeast of Athens stands the remains of the Doric-style Temple of Poseidon, dating back to the mid-fifth century BCE, where Poehler and Laurie filmed. “Talk about set decoration—you’re standing in front of something so amazing,” she says of the ruins at the end of Cape Sounion overlooking the Aegean Sea. The sacred place is even mentioned in Homer’s Odyssey, so needless to say, it’s also a busy tourist attraction. “We had to get there at the crack of dawn before the tours,” Poehler says, noting that the landmark’s staff was standing behind them counting down the minutes they had left. “That’s tough when you’re doing an emotional scene and you know someone wants to get you out of there.” But eventually they did have to open to the public as the cameras kept rolling. “It was funny to be pretending to have this conversation when there’s an American tourist behind you in the shot eating a bag of jelly beans.”

The port town of Monopoli provided the rich seaside vibe to double as Greece. Viswanathan says the initial montage where viewers are introduced to her character Dylan when she wakes up on a bench and asks for directions to the dig site was all in town, “which was so dreamy.” Poehler particularly loved the shopping scenes in its old town, including one with Laurie, shot at the hat shop Castrignano dal 1923 (sharp-eyed viewers will see it retains its Italian signage despite being set in Greece). “We wanted a place that Neville would go to pick out his hat for the year, and of course because it’s Italy, there was a beautiful old hat store in the middle of Monopoli and we used some of their hats.”

At Polignano a Mare, Poehler and co-creator Michael Schur kept open a local gelato stand for the public to enjoy free scoops.

Known for its dramatic scenery and crescent beaches, Polignano a Mare is best remembered to the duo for its most famous treat. “Gelato, so much gelato—Amy let the whole town eat gelato,” Viswanathan revealed. Indeed, after filming at a stand in town, Poehler and co-creator Michael Schur kept it open for the public to enjoy free scoops too. “Then Mike reminded me that I have not paid my half,” she admits. Despite being lactose intolerant, Viswanathan has a sweet spot for hazelnut, while Poehler is all about stracciatella, a refined form of chocolate chip. “I have to say, as an American, chocolate chip is very hard to find—it’s being replaced by mint chip,” to which her co-star replies, “ That’s so not right.”

The crew also headed inland to the hilltop town of Carovigno with a medieval fortress and a compact city center, which provided the bones for their set. “The locals were very interested in the fact that a production came in and shut down their town square and changed all of the store signs to Greek,” Poehler says. Viswanathan adds: “They were like, these Americans are confused—and lost!” But to get there, they also had to navigate the distinctly Italian way of driving. “It was intense—they come up really close and tailgate in a real way,” Poehler said. “You’ve got to get out of the way!”

Some of the Mediterranean scenery was recreated on a Universal Studios backlot in California.

Back on the Universal Studios backlot, set designer Dan Bishop—who’s worked on Mad Men and Parks and Recreation—recreated the Greek settings and dig site. “He and his team went over to Greece and got a bunch of local beer and signs, so when we were shooting in Los Angeles, it was really fun to be around all the stuff that felt authentic, from the colors and flowers to the buildings—it’s really important to get a feel of that.” But there was one twist that was distinctly Hollywood. “At times we could hear the Fast and Furious: [Hollywood Drift] roller coaster while we were shooting,” Poehler said of the theme park ride that opened in September, after they filmed. “We were hearing them do test runs—it’s open now, which is really exciting,” Viswanathan says. While she hadn't been on it yet, she commented, “the night is young.” As for Poehler, she's most happy with her feet firmly on the ground.

#6175. The Best Shopping in Athens for Crafts, Old and New

Resplendent, timeless Athens is no stranger to feats of invention and imagination. From the hand-carved marble stelae and temple friezes of the stately Acropolis to painted terra-cotta vessels unearthed throughout Attica, this is a city with millennia's worth of artistic output. You'll see this legacy on full display today in the museums and galleries that protect its artifacts. But, crucially, a new wave of makers are sculpting ceramics, weaving baskets, and vigorously curating heirlooms for the contemporary eye. There is plenty to discover in the historic center—at Monastiraki's sprawling outdoor market and ceramics studios, and Syntagma's perfumeries—though that's only the start. Athens may be among the world's oldest cities, but in bustling flea markets and quiet showrooms, its many creatives are paving the path forward.

The Acropolis rises over Monastiraki Square and Tzistarakis Mosque.

Following a stint in Paris designing for Jean Paul Gaultier and Kenzo over 25 years ago, Lito Karakostanoglou set up her jewelry brand, Lito, in Kolonaki. Treat the boutique and its nature-inspired offerings as a cabinet of curiosities. The showroom upstairs is your go-to for one-off pieces. Meanwhile, renowned family jeweler Lalaounis, on Voukourestiou Street, contains glittering collections that take cues from Nubian and Hellenistic art. Harder to find, but easier on the purse, is Neso Studio, in a prewar residential building on Praxitelous. Gold, gold-plated, and silver pieces are handmade there using wax casting techniques. It's best to check ahead for opening times.

Former managing director of label Yiorgos Eleftheriades, Yiorgos Mo turned his knack for collecting into Mo Vintage Athens in 2020. At his tiny shop in arty Koukaki, nab designer pieces from the 1970s to '90s—keep an eye out for Mugler rarities. A 20-minute walk north will take you to L'On, focusing on '80s and '90s garb; think Armani bodysuits and denim sprinkled amid garments from lesser-known Greek labels. Among Psirri's graffiti-sprayed shutters a few blocks over, shop custom-designed Mantility silk scarves and Homatino ceramics on display at Monument Hotel Athens. Nearby, hat workshop Savapile, led by Lisa Sarigiannidou, is the only remaining straw-hat maker in Greece still sewing Italian braid with traditional millinery techniques.

Sheep’s wool kilim and handloomed carpets are draped on a wall of Anthologist.

In eclectic Monastiraki, Mon Coin Studio—which features works from some 300 Greek ceramists—is equally varied. Its collaborative efforts culminate in three annual group shows, one of which is always dedicated to a region rich with a ceramics past such as Sifnos, Lesbos, or Crete. Head north to Vathi for blown-glass amphorae and handloomed throws at Anthologist; it's likely founder Andria Mitsakos will offer you tea and dates as you peruse. South of the Acropolis, shop at Ere Athens, where you can tuck into a cappuccino and banana bread (a perk of going to a store that's run by a pastry chef) while browsing locally made pottery neatly laid atop wood cabinets. Popular picks include paint-splattered cake stands by potter Nicola Fasano and painterly vases from Naked Summers.

Founded by brothers Giorgos and Apostolis Korres, The Naxos Apothecary near Syntagma Square creates tinctures and creams inspired by the Med. Scientific vessels and cloaked candles decorate the space, populated by staff wearing navy lab coats reminiscent of an old-school pharmacy. Leave no display case unexplored, then head upstairs for the herbal tea bar and an outpost of label Ancient Greek Sandals. Just as curated is perfume boutique and florist Phāon in Kolonaki, owned by art director and set designer duo Alexandros Kalogiros and Dimitra Louana Marlanti. Here, find soaps and scents from Astier de Villatte and Ormaie Paris, as well as golden candlesticks by Vasiliki and ceramic lotus flowers courtesy of Despina Charitonidi. Gnocchi the Jack Russell gives everyone a warm welcome.

Noting a lack of art and design bookshops in the city, graphic designer Stathis Mitropoulos and former fashion editor Andreas Kokkino opened their own. Hyper Hypo, meaning “above and below,” offers literature on photography, interior design, local culture, and more. Dimitris Papaioannou's Sketches From Life, drawn over three summers in Anafi, and Eleanor Lines's illustrated Doors of Kypseli stand out against the Aegean blue walls, while a pair of neon-lit eyes glow above the counter. Plus, Hyper Hypo's seasonal event programming and rare book pop-ups make a visit all the more memorable.

#6172. Delta Outage Delays Hundreds of Flights

A problem with one of Delta’s weight-and-balance systems delayed hundreds of flights Sunday, with backups most acute at the nation’s busiest airport.

According to FlightAware, Delta delayed over 2,100 flights Sunday and canceled 274.

Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport was the hardest hit, with about 700 flights delayed, though not all were Delta connections.

Delta said in a statement that its employees were using manual workarounds for baggage processing. It also said it would rebook customers on the next available flight and provide meals and hotel rooms where needed.

The FAA said on X that the problem was specific to Delta and had nothing to do with the agency’s air traffic control system, which crashed on Nov. 13.

Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system. These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems. Please check with Delta for the latest information. https://t.co/q4Fc59VMYg

The outage was resolved Sunday afternoon.

As of Monday morning, Delta’s delay rate was down to 6%.

While resolved fairly quickly, the system failure could hardly have come at a worse time. Millions of Americans are flying this week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, and there are concerns that technology outages could again snarl air traffic during the busiest time of the year. The single busiest day for air travel is expected to be Sunday, Nov. 29, after Thanksgiving.

#6171. Briggs and Riley Discount Codes | Black Friday 2026

I’ve often sung the praises of Briggs & Riley, and for good reason. It’s logged serious miles with me, from rolling across the cobblestones of Florence to the sweeping landscapes of Montana without so much as a loose wheel. Even after getting lost for two weeks at JFK Airport, it returned to me without one scratch.

Briggs & Riley’s commitment to reliability traces back to its founding in 1993 by luggage industry veteran Richard Costa, when the brand made its name with an innovative design and a straightforward promise: a lifetime repair guarantee that covers damage even if an airline is responsible.

Of course, luggage built this well rarely comes cheaply. Many of the brand’s most popular pieces sit firmly in investment territory, at around $500 and above. If you’ve traveled enough to know what makes a suitcase worth its weight, Briggs & Riley’s bestsellers speak for themselves. #6170. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

#6167. The Golden Rules of Affordable Family Travel, Illustrated by Mona Chalabi

My first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014. I had moved to the US in March of that year and had planned on working from home until a friend generously invited me to go spend the day with her family; an act of unguarded openness that I’ve realized is one of the many things that differentiates Americans from Brits. As soon as we got off the train in Cambridge, Massachusetts, I realized that even though my friend lived in a nasty, overcrowded apartment in Brooklyn, she came from a family that had immense wealth. After dinner, as I helped wash plates in the kitchen, my friend’s mum asked her why she wouldn’t just move into the lovely building they had bought for her. She turned beet red and handed me another dirty plate without looking at me.

Take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions. Of course, there’s the annual reminder of colonization which requires a careful forgetting of the people who have been colonized. And then there’s the financial aspect of it. At first blush, it seems like the least capitalist holiday of the year—there isn’t the expense of Christmas or Hanukkah gift-giving or the extravagance of Halloween candy. Yet the holiday also marks the start of one of the year's busiest travel seasons when families are taking great expense to reunite, vacation, and explore outside of their every day lives.

As we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in New York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe. All of these stories say something about the wealth of the person writing it, whether or not they wanted to reveal that information. I’m obsessed with getting to the truth about someone’s class (it’s why I wrote my book on the subject), and so these family dispatches, which serve as equal parts advice and confession, are a treat I’ll come back to when I’m not busy washing a rich family’s plates. —Mona Chalabi, Pulitzer Prize-winning writer and illustrator

Keep reading for the tips and tricks of affordable family travel, road-tested by the experts and illustrated by Mona Chalabi.

I know the secret to parenting and I’m willing to share it: snacks. Snacks are everything—they’re an activity, a mood changer, and a window into culture for kids. Hit a local farmers market on your first day or if you’re somewhere truly out of their comfort zone even a local convenience store—like 7-Eleven in Tokyo—for something that can feel both familiar and novel. If your hotel room has a refrigerator you can store any pre-cut fruit that you buy, or opt for items that don’t require refrigeration like apples, bananas, and clementines. Bring a lightweight backpack, refill each morning, and watch the hangry meltdowns (mostly) vanish. —Dana Kravis, global executive director, CNT video

Last December in London, we stayed in a quaint Airbnb in Primrose Hill and explored different neighborhoods on foot. When our kids, then eight and three, got tired, we hopped on a double-decker bus and headed upstairs, hoping for front seats. Suddenly, getting home became an amusement park ride: Christmas lights, bustling streets, panoramic views. The kids loved it; as a photographer, I loved the vantage point. London caps daily bus fares when you use the same card or phone, and children under 11 ride free. We’ve done this in Singapore, too. Our rule: skip the sightseeing tour (or Uber) and make public transportation part of the family adventure. —Tanveer Badal, photographer

Breakfast is where family vacations are made, or broken. My moody teenagers can’t be pried out of bed no matter what city they wake up in, so instead of wringing my uncaffeinated hands and hoping to get us all on the same schedule, I just bring my own breakfast, coffee included. Whether in Paris, Rome, or a tent, you will find me hand-grinding my coffee beans, brewing a pour-over, and snacking on a pastry left over from the previous day while I peruse headlines. Avoiding the time and expense of a sit-down breakfast, and indulging in a bit of morning self-care, means we can focus on the adventures and meals we are actually going to remember. —Chris Morocco, food director of Bon Appétit and Epicurious

My parents and I meet in Aruba every winter for a family vacation that’s warm and relaxing when everyone else is cold and miserable. It’s a classic only child/parents trip where we spend most of our time eating lunch talking about where we’re going to eat dinner. We spend our days mostly just reading parallel to each other. I’ve never been an e-reader user, so I have to bring several physical books to read to get me through the week. The key is that my mom and I have some shared taste in books, so when we finish our own we can swap and save ourselves buying extra books (or lugging even heavier luggage through the airport). —Alison Leiby, comedian and writer

Finding creative ways to entertain wiggly one-year-olds with limited attention spans can be daunting, but it turns out all you need is a good window. From London to California, staying in rooms on low floors with windows overlooking lots of activity below has resulted in seemingly endless engagement—waving at commuters striding by or golfers strolling a few feet away? Bonus points if the room has curtains with electronic controls—that guarantees an extra hour of ooohs and aaahs, at least. —Sarah Khan, contributing editor

I have a thing for seeing “The World’s Biggest or Oldest,” and so here we were at Missouri’s Oldest Wooden Suspension Bridge. “Don’t tell your mom,” I said to my kids, because any bridge that was built from wood during the Civil War should be treated with caution—and, also, all good dad stories start that way. We started up the van, piled everyone in, and began the adventure. The wood cracked and echoed as we drove over the river. It sounded like a popping spinal cord. We swayed, and for a moment, I actually questioned myself. I should have just taken them to the park. Thankfully, I can now confidently say that Missouri’s oldest wooden suspension bridge can hold the weight of a mini-van. —Shannon Carpenter, humorist

New York is an expensive city and the best way to keep it cheap is to throw petty cash at it. Instead of buying tickets to an overpriced kid’s experience, I give my children a few twenty dollar bills and take them to Chinatown for a shopping spree. They love the atrocious arcade, and there are fake Labubus, squishy dumplings, a plastic “jade” green dragon that my son now keeps on his bedside, and a 'gold' necklace my daughter thinks is treasure. —Stephanie Danler, author

As a seasoned travel writer, I know that any hotel that’s gotten media coverage is often pushing $1,000/night. My trick for affordable family lodging is loading up Google maps, figuring out which area we’re going to stay in, and picking a cheerful place with good reviews in the $250 range. It’s almost never one you’ve heard of, but they’re always clean and cheerful, usually family-owned, and we always leave with big hugs and promises to keep in touch. That doesn’t happen at the Georges V. My kids (12 and 8) loved a converted windmill in Rome, a townhouse two blocks from the Rijksmuseum and—most recently—an orange grove near Siracusa where they spent so much time chasing the owner’s cats they even forgot Wi-Fi existed. A steal at any price! —Priyanka Mattoo, filmmaker and author

People tell you about a million things you “need” before your baby is born, but there's one that has come in the most handy, and I've had a true love/hate relationship with it since day one: A travel car seat. After a ton of research—some may say over-research—we bought a Maxi Cosi Romi. It's rated high for safety, but it's also easy to strap into a car and also an airplane. We always bring it on the airplane, and that's where the headache comes in. While the Maxi Cosi Romi is considered lightweight, it's also big and bulky, and the only way to get it through the airport and onto the plane is by wearing it in a special backpack. I'm pretty sure that I'm one of the most annoying people in any airport as I'm walking through it since I can't really see if I'm bumping into people in the TSA line or getting to the gate. The thing is that, after I considered the numbers, it's actually a really wise investment because most rental car places charge anywhere from $10 to $15 a day to rent a car seat, so we've already started saving money because of it. Now, that's about a hundred or more dollars we're not spending when we go out of town and bring the Maxi. It's wildly annoying and inconvenient, and I look like I'm wearing a jetpack as I'm walking through the airport, but it's worth it. —Jason Diamond, 'Figuring' family columnist at The Cut

I️ live in Brooklyn where people leave really good stuff out on the street. Once I️ found one of those giant extra storage containers you put on top of your car. I️ haven't found the time to figure out how to put it on top of the car; it's been taking up valuable space in my home for over a year. The other day, I️ found another one that looked even fancier. I️ dragged it home. One day, ideally before our car gets too old to work anymore, I️ will figure this out, then get rid of the extra one somehow (do I️ need to call 311?). After that, my husband, our two kids, our dog, our parakeets and I️ will pack up everything we could possibly need to rent a house somewhere for a week or two. I️ have my eye on Block Island or Martha's Vineyard. —Liana Finck, cartoonist and author

From bustling markets to neighborhood festivals, I've learned that some of the best family entertainment happens in the streets. In Oaxaca, my four-year-old was mesmerized by calendas, raucous community processions with brass bands, towering puppets called monos de calenda, and rag-covered revelers known as tiliches. Paradegoers tossed my kid candy, fireworks exploded overhead, and the party raged late into the night. We didn't pay a peso. Before booking pricey family activities, research local festivals, celebrations, and public performances. Sometimes the most exciting show in town is happening right on the sidewalk. —Ashlea Halpern, contributing editor

On our last family vacation to Rajasthan, a passionfruit lassi from our five-star hotel nearly ruined the trip. We’re talking emergency roadside bathroom stops and several days of Zofran. We’ve been taking our kids—Vijay, Vik, and Meera—to Rajasthan since they were babies; they’re teenagers now. And we’ve learned one unexpected lesson: the sickest we’ve ever been in India was after eating at our five-star hotel. More than once.

So we’ve adopted a new philosophy: pack the right medicine and embrace street food. In Jaipur, Vineet Sharma, founder of Jaipur Walks, led us on a street food tour around the bustling market, introducing us to piping-hot pyaaz kachori and creamy, saffron-rich kulfi. His advice? Choose clean stalls with high turnover, and favor food cooked fresh and served hot over raw offerings. At busy stalls, food is often prepared continuously and served straight from the heat—sometimes a more reassuring bet than a meal at a luxury hotel or high-end restaurant. And if your stomach’s going to revolt, at least make the meal memorable. —Christine Chitnis, author and photographer

This may not be the most popular piece of advice, and I doubt it'll be the most obvious: take your kids overseas during school time. Hear me out: the longer you can stretch your child's travels beyond the limited school holidays when ticket prices always soar, the better for your wallet. Of course, every parent needs to set their own boundary on what and how much school their kind can miss in the name of travel but I feel, especially at a young age, the benefits of the trip outweigh the additional days in the classroom. As I am writing this, I am preparing to leave tomorrow with my first grader for Italy for a week. We are cooking up plans to take our two kids on a long haul trip to the southern hemisphere that'll cut into a week of school. I have heard from more than one expert that Disney especially, should be done when your kids are young, and outside normal school holidays if you want to get great value. I don't do it often but I do balance the guilt with rules—we have to read every day, and do exercises from a homework packet to keep on top of the basics. One day, and soon, I know I won't want to do this much more. But for now, I'm taking every chance to do so. —Erin Florio, global features director

#6166. White House budget aide Ueland slated to head GAO

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

The nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters said.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

"I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

"To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad."

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

Before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

DeBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

#6163. New aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the new request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

There is a lot to love about JetBlue. The airline offers generous legroom, tasty snacks and free Wi-Fi. It also has a fairly straightforward loyalty program.

JetBlue TrueBlue points are easy to earn through flights, partner activity, cobranded credit cards and transferable rewards. They are also easy to redeem because any seat on a JetBlue-operated flight can be booked with points, and there are no blackout dates. The program has become more useful through an expanding network of airline partners, including the Blue Sky partnership with United Airlines.

Here is everything you need to know about the JetBlue TrueBlue loyalty program.

JetBlue serves more than 100 destinations throughout the U.S., Latin America, Canada, the Caribbean and Europe. The airline isn’t part of any global alliance but has a growing roster of airline partners.

With JetBlue being one of the youngest major airlines in the U.S., the TrueBlue loyalty program is a relative newcomer to the points and miles world. The program is revenue-based, so earning and redeeming points are typically tied to ticket prices. However, there are also many ways to earn JetBlue points without even getting on an airplane.

TrueBlue points do not expire. Points Pooling also lets between two and seven friends or family members combine their balances, although members must contribute all of their points to the pool while participating.

Related: How to change or cancel a JetBlue flight

JetBlue isn't part of a global alliance, but TrueBlue members can earn and redeem points with the following airline partners.

JetBlue says earning and redeeming with Cape Air are temporarily unavailable while it updates its systems.

Blue Sky lets TrueBlue members earn points and Tiles on eligible United-operated flights booked through JetBlue and redeem TrueBlue points for United flights through JetBlue. Mosaic members also receive reciprocal perks on United, including priority boarding, one complimentary checked bag, preferred seating and Economy Plus seats at check-in. Base fares receive the above benefits except seat selection, and the partnership does not provide reciprocal lounge access.

You can join TrueBlue for free online, starting at the “basic” level. The four published tiers of JetBlue elite status are:

JetBlue uses Tiles to track progress toward "Perks You Pick" — a selection of benefits you can choose from after earning a set number of Tiles — and Mosaic status. You earn 1 Tile for every:

Government-imposed taxes, government-imposed fees and travel insurance do not earn Tiles. Tiles are a status metric and cannot be redeemed for travel.

This means you could earn elite status entirely through credit card spending, through qualifying travel spending or with a combination of the two.

Before reaching Mosaic 1, members can choose a different Perks You Pick benefit at 10, 20, 30 and 40 Tiles. Through Jan. 31, 2027, the choices include early boarding, priority security, a complimentary first inflight alcoholic drink, double points per dollar spent on a JetBlue Vacations package or 5,000 bonus points.

You can pick each of these only once, even if you earn all four Tile amounts.

Related: JetBlue changes its boarding order with new groups

Mosaic members also choose one Perks You Pick benefit at each status level. Current choices include a pet fee waiver, IHG One Rewards Platinum Elite status, Mint Suite selection priority, FoundersCard Blue membership, a $99 statement credit for an eligible JetBlue credit card, a 20-Tile bonus for the member or another TrueBlue member and 15,000 bonus points.

Changes are coming in 2027: Beginning Feb. 1, members will receive a new tier-specific Perks You Pick menu at each Mosaic milestone, may select the same perk again at a later milestone and will have 60 days to make each choice. A pet fee waiver will become an automatic Mosaic 2 benefit, while eligible JetBlue Premier Card members will gain additional card-exclusive choices.

The information for the JetBlue Premier Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Separately, when BlueFirst service begins Dec. 8, all Mosaic members and one companion on the same reservation will be eligible for complimentary, space-available upgrades on eligible BlueFirst flights. Main Base and EvenMore Base fares will not be eligible.

Related: JetBlue announces first-class upgrades and new elite benefits for 2027

There are many ways to save up for a JetBlue award ticket.

When flying JetBlue, you’ll earn TrueBlue points based on the ticket cost, the fare type and whether you book directly with JetBlue.

JetBlue now sells Main, EvenMore, BlueFirst and Mint experiences, with Base and Flex variants available in most cabins. Base fares earn 1 base point per dollar spent, plus 1 point per dollar when booked on jetblue.com or through the JetBlue app. Standard and Flex fares earn 3 base points per dollar spent, plus 3 points per dollar when booked directly.

You can earn TrueBlue points on eligible flights operated by United Airlines, Condor, Etihad Airways, Icelandair, Qatar Airways, Singapore Airlines and South African Airways.

United is different from JetBlue's other partners. TrueBlue members earn 5 points per dollar spent on eligible United-operated flights booked through JetBlue; government-imposed taxes, fees and surcharges are excluded. Eligible United flights credited to TrueBlue also earn Tiles. For most other partners, earning depends on the operating airline, the booking class and the distance flown.

You can find each partner’s earning chart in JetBlue’s partner directory.

There are several ways to earn TrueBlue points without flying:

You can also purchase JetBlue points or pool them with other members.

JetBlue also offers Points On Repeat subscriptions. These provide a set number of TrueBlue points each month. Higher tiers add a flight-earning accelerator, while the top tier also includes a 10% rebate on eligible JetBlue award flights. Compare the subscription cost with the value you expect to receive before enrolling.

JetBlue has four cobranded credit cards, all issued by Barclays:

TrueBlue is also a transfer partner of seven flexible rewards currencies at the following transfer rates:

Related: Credit card transfer partners: Guide to transferring points and miles to airlines and hotels

JetBlue uses a dynamic pricing scheme for its own flights, so redemptions are pretty straightforward. You can redeem points for any seat on any JetBlue-operated flight across its entire route network. The more a flight costs in cash, the more it will cost in points.

According to TPG’s November 2026 valuations, TrueBlue points are worth 1.35 cents each on average. To calculate the value of a specific award, subtract any taxes and fees from the cash price, divide the result by the number of points required and multiply by 100. Mint and Cash + Points bookings may offer less value, while some partner awards can offer more.

To check award availability, search for flights on JetBlue’s website as you normally would and check the “Use TrueBlue points” option at the top of the search box. Base fares can now be booked with points, although JetBlue charges $150 per person to change or cancel a Base award.

Cash + Points bookings start at 500 points and are available for JetBlue-operated flights and eligible JetBlue Vacations packages. This option can be useful if you are short on points, but it often delivers less value than a standard award. Cash + Points bookings are not available for partner airline awards.

TrueBlue points can also cover certain seat assignments, checked bags, pet fees and priority security. You can redeem points through TrueBlue Travel for eligible hotel stays and car rentals as well.

In addition to using your points for JetBlue flights, you can redeem TrueBlue points on JetBlue's site for eligible flights operated by United Airlines, Condor, Etihad Airways, Icelandair, Qatar Airways and China Airlines. Cape Air redemptions are temporarily paused.

Partner award availability can be limited, and each one-way award must be operated by a single carrier. Frustratingly, you cannot combine a JetBlue flight and a partner flight on the same one-way award, although you can book the outbound and return on different airlines.

A Points Pooling account can have two to seven members and must include at least one person age 21 or older. Members contribute 100% of the points they earn after joining. The pool leader and anyone granted redemption privileges can use pooled points without the other members' permission, so only pool with people you trust. A member who leaves takes their remaining points balance with them.

Related: Family points pooling: How to transfer and maximize your rewards

While you’re unlikely to get incredible value from your points, the JetBlue TrueBlue program is still useful for many travelers. TrueBlue points are among the easiest domestic airline points to earn and redeem. JetBlue-operated awards do not require an award chart and have no blackout dates, though partner award availability can be restricted.

JetBlue's expanded partner network makes TrueBlue more globally useful. New transfer partnerships with Rove and Bilt also make it easier to top up a balance. JetBlue's revenue-based pricing usually limits the opportunity for exceptional value on its own flights, but straightforward redemptions and occasional high-value partner awards make TrueBlue worth understanding.

#6161. Storms on Both Coasts Threaten Thanksgiving Travel

Powerful storms bringing high winds and the potential for flooding could seriously disrupt commercial air travel in the U.S. during the single busiest week of the year.

Forecasters are warning that storm systems will likely strike parts of the South, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast, as well as Northern California and the Pacific Northwest. These regions are home to some of the nation’s busiest airports, through which millions of American travelers will pass this week en route to visit family and friends for Thanksgiving on Thursday.

In the Northeast, the remnants of a weakened, disorganized system were still clearing out on Monday. A much stronger storm is expected to develop in the Gulf of Mexico between Monday and Tuesday, impact parts of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic Wednesday, and slam into the New York metro area and New England on Thanksgiving Day.

According to an advisory from the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center, strong wind gusts up to 50 mph will be felt from the Carolinas to Maine. Flooding and beach erosion could be seen in coastal areas due to the already high tides.

WPC has initiated Key Messages for a Thanksgiving Coastal Storm that is expected to impact the U.S. East Coast. pic.twitter.com/pdQuU4U4yG

Americans traveling from, through, or to these areas should prepare for the possibility of flooded roads, damage from high winds, and power outages, the agency said.

NYC Emergency Management said Sunday that the storm could bring gusts of 40 to 45 mph and about one to two inches of rain to the city.

For New York and New England, the storm will be at its strongest Thursday evening. Parts of the Adirondacks and northern New England could see ice and snow mixed in with rain.

In California, Oregon, and Washington, residents still recovering from flooding last week could be hit again by rain and strong winds. A new system is expected to move in Tuesday and Wednesday; combined with the “king tides,” the storm could cause flooding up and down the West Coast.

The impact is expected to be most severe between Portland, Oregon, and San Francisco. San Francisco’s mayor said residents should take the forecasts seriously and consider not traveling for the holiday.

The Sierra Nevada, meanwhile, will see fresh snow, meteorologists said.

Over six million people are expected to fly within the U.S. this week for Thanksgiving. The surge is already underway, with many carriers adding flights to accommodate the increased traffic. American Airlines earlier this month projected its busiest Thanksgiving week since before the COVID-19 pandemic; that prediction could hold true for other U.S. airlines as well.

AirlineGeeks will continue to monitor weather conditions and provide updates as the week progresses.

#6158. ITA Airways Discount Code: 10% Off This Black Friday | Condé Nast Traveler

There’s never a bad time to embrace la dolce vita and head to Italy for a dreamy vacation filled with pasta dinners, languorous afternoons sipping wine, and views that belong on a postcard. One of the easiest ways to get there is by zipping over to the beautiful region via the country’s airline carrier, ITA Airways. Whether you’re leaving from the East or West Coast, ITA Airways serves top hubs in the US like NYC, Boston, Atlanta, and San Francisco. Plus, the airline connects travelers with top cities all across the world outside of Italy, from Delhi to Paris to Dakar, Senegal.

Personally, I’m a big fan of long-haul flights—they give you enough time to take a break before or after an intense vacation and let you spend six hours straight watching movies without feeling guilty. And when your final destination is somewhere dreamy like Florence or Trieste, your flight is full of excitement and anticipation. Whether you’re popping between Italian cities, crossing oceans, or traversing continents, ITA Airways has the tools to get you from A to B in style. Read on for the best ways to save on your travels, including ITA Airways promo codes, Black Friday discounts, and offerings to keep more money in your pocket next time you fly ITA Airways.

ITA Airways is participating in Black Friday this year, so if you've been thinking about planning a vacation, let this be your sign. From now through November 30, you can use the ITA Airways Black Friday promo code CYBERDAYS to score 10% off your base fare for one-way or round-trip tickets departing from the US and going to any ITA Airways destination, for travel from December 1, 2026, to March 22, 2027. Note that the code only works for economy class tickets and is not valid for multi-leg itineraries. Visit the promo page to find your next big flight.

ITA Airways frequent flyer and rewards program, Miles & More, opens even more doors for saving big. The airline shares its frequent flyer and rewards program with Lufthansa Group, so you’ll be able to earn across all airlines. Plus, it’s free to join and start saving.

There are three membership tiers: Frequent Traveller, Senator, and HON Circle. To achieve Frequent Traveller status, guests must earn 650 points and 325 qualifying points in a calendar year. While you’ll earn regular points when flying on all travel classes across an array of Star Alliance airlines, you can only earn qualifying points when you fly on the following airlines: Air Dolomiti, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, Discover Airlines, Eurowings, ITA Airways, Lufthansa, SWISS, Croatia Airlines, LOT Polish Airlines, and Luxair. Benefits include business lounge access, the opportunity to get up to 50% extra miles that can be redeemed for additional rewards, and increased free baggage allowance.

To achieve Senator status, you must earn 2,000 points and 1,000 qualifying points in return for benefits like first-class check-in, priority boarding, and access to Senator/Star Alliance Gold lounges. As for HON Circle? That costs a whopping 6,000 HON points, which can only be earned by flying business or first class on select airline partners. Perks include access to first-class lounges, exclusive chauffeur and transfer services, and free upgrade vouchers. Miles & More members can also earn up to 25% cashback on intercontinental award travel bookings departing from the US, or up to 15% cashback on general intercontinental itineraries.

Those between the ages of 12 and 25 are eligible for ITA Airways youth fares to help cut down on travel costs. Simply head to the airline’s Youth Offers page and pop in your desired arrival and departure dates and locations, and scroll through the plentiful options. Discounts will be applied directly to your booking when made through this page (it will say “youth fare” under the correct price), and you’ll be able to follow through with your booking as usual.

Offers are only eligible for those who will be 12–25 years old on the date of travel, and passengers may need to prove their eligibility upon boarding (so have your ID ready). This discounted fare is only valid for flights to destinations in Europe and is not applicable to unaccompanied minors under 14; 14-year-olds may travel unaccompanied to domestic locations only.

If your ITA Airways discount code isn’t working, don’t fret. There are a couple of things you can do to get your code up and working. The first thing to check is whether you’re applying your promo code to the correct fare class—ITA Airways discount codes are often class-specific, so for example, basic economy fares may not apply. Also be sure to check your discount code to confirm your proposed booking is for an eligible route, not during a blackout date, and hasn’t expired. If all else fails, don’t forget to double-check your code for any spacing errors or mistaken capitalizations.

It's also worth keeping in mind that, like for most other products and services, discount codes do not work on taxes and fees. Your discount may look a bit different when you actually book than during advertising, since the percentage is only applied to the base fare with taxes and fees added on afterward.
